one_line_idea: Claimed viewpoint invariance of self-supervised ViT features collapses at a measurable camera-baseline knee, and the knee position, not average similarity, predicts a backbone's 3D utility.
problem: Self-supervised 2D features are widely reused for cross-view correspondence and 3D distillation, but the supporting evidence is dominated by narrow-baseline or object-centric pairs.
core_hypothesis: Feature view-invariance is mostly co-visible texture matching and decays nonlinearly with viewpoint change: there is a baseline angle beyond which correspondence utility drops toward chance while narrow-baseline metrics stay high.
falsifiable_prediction: On registered RGB-D scan sequences, reprojection-verified nearest-neighbor match recall for the same 3D points will drop by more than half between the 10-20 degree and 50-60 degree relative-viewpoint bins for frozen SSL ViTs.
why_important: Pose, mapping, and 3D-distillation pipelines budget the number of views assuming smooth feature degradation; a hard knee changes view planning and tells us where 3D-aware fine-tuning should concentrate.
why_possibly_novel: Baseline-stratified correspondence evaluation against ground-truth geometry, with the knee angle reported as a first-class backbone property, does not appear to be a standard published protocol (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample co-visible 3D points from registered indoor scans (e.g., ScanNet-style data), bin image pairs by relative viewpoint angle controlling for co-visibility, and plot feature-match recall at a fixed reprojection threshold versus angle for 3-4 frozen backbones.
main_risk: Occlusion, motion blur, and resolution confound with baseline; co-visibility must be verified from geometry, not assumed.
community_default_belief: Self-supervised ViT features are treated as approximately viewpoint-invariant descriptors whose quality varies smoothly with viewing conditions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The invariances were learned from 2D crops and photometric augmentations of single images, so genuine out-of-plane rotation is off the training manifold and need not degrade gracefully.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-afternoon: 100 scan image pairs binned by viewpoint angle, one frozen backbone, recall-versus-angle curve from GT-geometry-verified matches.
kill_threshold: Kill if recall at 50-60 degrees is within 20% relative of recall at 10-20 degrees, or if the recall-vs-angle curve shows no knee (max local slope ratio below 2).

one_line_idea: Geometric information in vision foundation models peaks in middle transformer blocks, so standard last-layer feature extraction systematically understates and misranks the 3D awareness of 2D backbones.
problem: 3D-awareness probing and feature-lifting pipelines overwhelmingly read features from the final transformer block, inheriting a convention from semantic tasks.
core_hypothesis: Depth, surface-normal, and correspondence information is concentrated in middle blocks and is progressively discarded by later blocks that specialize toward semantic abstraction, and the peak layer shifts with pretraining objective.
falsifiable_prediction: Layer-wise linear probes for monocular depth and normals will peak at 50-75% relative network depth for contrastive and image-text models, with a probe-error gap versus the last layer that exceeds the gap between competing backbones at their respective best layers.
why_important: If layer choice matters more than backbone choice, published 3D-awareness rankings of foundation models are protocol artifacts and cheap gains are available by re-reading existing checkpoints.
why_possibly_novel: Layer-stratified 3D probing exists for isolated models, but using peak-layer geometry probes to re-rank backbone families and showing rank flips versus last-layer protocol appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze 4-6 public backbones, train identical linear depth and normal probes on every 4th block on one indoor and one outdoor RGB-D dataset, and compare peak-layer versus last-layer probe metrics and cross-backbone rankings.
main_risk: Linear probes may be too weak to expose geometry that is present but nonlinearly encoded, understating late-layer geometry.
community_default_belief: The last layer of a strong foundation model is the best single representation for downstream dense tasks including geometric ones.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training objectives that reward semantic invariance actively remove pose- and depth-variant information in the final blocks, a loss that semantic benchmarks never detect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One backbone, probes at 4 layers on one RGB-D dataset, one GPU-day: check whether any middle layer beats the last layer on depth probe error by the kill margin.
kill_threshold: Kill if no middle layer improves depth-probe AbsRel by at least 10% relative over the last layer on both datasets, or if backbone rankings are identical under last-layer and peak-layer protocols.

one_line_idea: Learned feature upsamplers make features look sharper while corrupting the sub-pixel geometric signal, so pipelines that match or triangulate upsampled features get worse 3D estimates than bilinear baselines.
problem: High-resolution feature upsampling modules are increasingly inserted before geometric uses of foundation features, validated mainly on semantic benchmarks and visual sharpness.
core_hypothesis: Upsamplers trained with image-guided objectives snap feature boundaries to intensity edges, which hallucinates spatial precision: the apparent localization is inherited from the guidance image, not the feature content, and it biases correspondence residuals near depth discontinuities.
falsifiable_prediction: On wide-baseline correspondence with ground-truth geometry, matches from guided-upsampled features will show larger mean epipolar residuals near depth edges than matches from bilinearly upsampled features of the same backbone, despite better-looking feature maps.
why_important: Sub-pixel accuracy is what SfM, calibration, and reconstruction pipelines actually consume; a component that improves appearance while degrading residuals will silently harm 3D systems as it spreads.
why_possibly_novel: Upsampler evaluation via epipolar and triangulation residuals rather than downstream semantic scores appears untested (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix one backbone; extract correspondences on standard two-view geometry data via nearest neighbor plus sub-pixel refinement using (a) bilinear and (b) learned guided upsampling; compare epipolar residual distributions stratified by distance to depth edges.
main_risk: Effect may be upsampler-specific; needs 2-3 distinct upsampler designs before a general claim.
community_default_belief: Sharper, edge-aligned feature maps are strictly better inputs for any dense downstream task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Edge alignment is a semantic prior; geometry lives in phase-like sub-pixel structure that guided filtering overwrites with intensity-edge structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: 50 image pairs with GT poses, one backbone, bilinear versus one public upsampler, compare median epipolar residual near depth edges.
kill_threshold: Kill if guided upsampling does not increase near-edge median epipolar residual by at least 15% relative in at least 2 of 3 tested upsamplers.

family_fingerprint.subject_system: feature upsampling modules over frozen backbones

one_line_idea: Image-text contrastive features are not geometry-poor: controlling for resolution and probe capacity, their coarse depth-ordering knowledge matches self-supervised features, and the reported gap is a protocol artifact.
problem: The community narrative says contrastive image-text pretraining discards geometry while self-distillation preserves it, based on probe comparisons that differ in resolution, token count, and probe capacity across model families.
core_hypothesis: Much of the measured 3D-awareness gap between image-text and self-distilled backbones is explained by input resolution and effective patch density rather than the pretraining objective.
falsifiable_prediction: After matching effective token grids and probe capacity, the ordinal-depth probe gap between image-text and self-distilled ViTs will shrink by at least half relative to the standard-protocol gap on the same data.
why_important: Objective-level conclusions steer pretraining investments for 3D; if the gap is protocol-induced, cheap resolution interventions matter more than switching objectives.
why_possibly_novel: Resolution-and-capacity-matched 3D probing across objective families, with a variance decomposition into objective versus protocol factors, appears not to have been published (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take paired public checkpoints of comparable size, evaluate ordinal depth-pair accuracy probes at matched token grids and matched probe parameter counts on one indoor and one outdoor dataset, and decompose the gap.
main_risk: Public checkpoints confound objective with data distribution; needs at least one same-data controlled pair to be conclusive.
community_default_belief: Language-supervised pretraining fundamentally sacrifices geometric detail relative to self-supervised visual objectives.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Depth ordering is learnable from monocular pictorial cues that captions weakly but consistently supervise, and probe studies rarely equalize the plumbing that dominates dense readout quality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: two checkpoints, ordinal depth probes at two matched resolutions each, gap-versus-protocol table.
kill_threshold: Kill if the matched-protocol gap remains above 75% of the standard-protocol gap, confirming the objective-level explanation.

one_line_idea: Foundation features carry a systematic metric-scale bias inherited from the crop-scale distribution of pretraining augmentations, measurable as a predictable error in apparent-size judgments.
problem: Multi-crop and random-resize augmentations expose models to a specific distribution of object scales, but nobody characterizes what scale prior this stamps into the features.
core_hypothesis: Frozen features encode apparent object scale with a bias toward the pretraining crop-scale distribution: probes estimating physical size or distance will show errors correlated with the mismatch between test-time object scale and the augmentation scale density.
falsifiable_prediction: A size-estimation probe on frozen features will show error that is a U-shaped function of apparent object scale, with the minimum near the modal augmentation scale, consistent across backbones sharing augmentation recipes and shifted for backbones with different recipes.
why_important: Scale priors propagate into every metric-3D system built on 2D backbones; knowing the bias direction enables correction layers and better augmentation design for geometry-heavy uses.
why_possibly_novel: Linking augmentation hyperparameters to a quantitative scale-estimation bias curve in downstream probes appears unexplored (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render controlled scenes with objects at parameterized apparent scales, train size/distance probes on frozen features from backbones with documented augmentation recipes, and regress probe error against distance from the augmentation scale mode.
main_risk: Public models differ in many factors beyond augmentation; a small controlled pretraining run may be needed for causal attribution.
community_default_belief: Augmentation choices affect invariance and semantic quality but wash out as benign implementation details in large-scale pretraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale is exactly the variable augmentations manipulate most aggressively, so it is the variable most likely to carry a systematic imprint rather than washing out.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: synthetic renders across 8 scale bins, two backbones with different documented crop policies, probe-error-versus-scale curves.
kill_threshold: Kill if probe error curves are flat within noise (max/min bin error ratio below 1.2) or uncorrelated with the documented augmentation scale distributions.

one_line_idea: Under controlled synthetic viewpoint sweeps, generative-diffusion features are not more multi-view consistent than contrastive features once texture density is controlled, contradicting a growing assumption in 3D distillation work.
problem: A popular assumption holds that features from generative models are more 3D-consistent because generation requires implicit geometry, but comparisons are made on uncontrolled real images.
core_hypothesis: Apparent cross-view stability advantages of diffusion features come from their sensitivity to low-frequency appearance, which correlates across views for texture-poor content, not from superior geometric encoding.
falsifiable_prediction: On rendered viewpoint sweeps of textured versus texture-poor assets, the cross-view feature stability advantage of diffusion features over contrastive features will appear only in texture-poor conditions and vanish or invert for high-texture assets at matched spatial resolution.
why_important: Choice of 2D teacher for 3D feature fields and correspondence distillation is being made on this belief; a texture-confound explanation changes teacher selection and hybrid strategies.
why_possibly_novel: Texture-controlled synthetic viewpoint-sweep evaluation of feature families with a stability-by-texture interaction analysis appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render viewpoint orbits of public 3D assets stratified by texture statistics, compute view-pair feature similarity for matched 3D surface points across feature families, and test the family-by-texture interaction.
main_risk: Rendered imagery may be out-of-distribution for both families in ways that reorder them; a small real multi-view control set is needed.
community_default_belief: Generative pretraining yields features with better 3D consistency than discriminative or contrastive pretraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generation quality mostly requires local appearance modeling; cross-view identity of surface points is never directly supervised in either family, so neither has a principled advantage.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 50 assets in two texture bins, two feature families, view-pair cosine similarity at GT-corresponding points, interaction test.
kill_threshold: Kill if diffusion features hold a stability advantage of at least 10% relative in both texture bins, which would support the community belief.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: surface texture density under controlled viewpoint sweep

one_line_idea: A measurable fraction of reported 3D awareness in ViT probes is absolute positional-embedding leakage: probes read where a patch is in the frame, not what geometry the features encode.
problem: Depth and normal probes on frozen ViTs are interpreted as measuring geometric content of learned features, but ViT tokens also carry absolute position information that correlates with depth in typical photographs (ground below, sky above).
core_hypothesis: A nontrivial share of probe performance survives feature ablation but not position ablation, meaning current 3D-awareness numbers overstate the geometry actually encoded in appearance features.
falsifiable_prediction: Depth probes re-evaluated under vertical-flip test-time transforms and randomized crop offsets will lose a disproportionate share of accuracy compared to semantic probes on the same tokens, and a position-only baseline probe will explain a nontrivial fraction of reported depth-probe skill.
why_important: 3D-awareness leaderboards inform which backbones get lifted into 3D pipelines; if position leakage inflates scores, rankings and conclusions about pretraining objectives are distorted.
why_possibly_novel: Position-only baselines and position-randomization controls appear absent from published 3D-awareness probing protocols (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 3 backbones, train (a) standard depth probes, (b) probes on position-randomized tokens, and (c) position-only probes with no image content, on one indoor and one outdoor dataset; decompose probe skill into content and position components.
main_risk: Aggressive position randomization can degrade features themselves, over-attributing skill to position; needs careful crop-based controls.
community_default_belief: Probe accuracy on frozen features measures the geometric information content of the learned representation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Natural image composition makes vertical position alone a strong depth predictor, and probes will exploit any shortcut available.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: position-only probe on one dataset; if it reaches a substantial fraction of full-probe skill the leakage concern is live.
kill_threshold: Kill if the position-only probe explains under 10% of full-probe depth accuracy and position randomization changes probe error by under 5% relative.

one_line_idea: Textureless-surface correspondence failure of foundation features is a token-granularity artifact, and dense overlapping-stride re-extraction recovers most of it without any retraining.
problem: Feature-based matching is believed to fail intrinsically on textureless surfaces, pushing systems toward expensive learned matchers or active sensing.
core_hypothesis: Much of the failure is quantization: coarse patch grids average away weak shading gradients that do carry correspondence signal, so densely re-extracting features with overlapping strides and aggregating them recovers usable matches on low-texture regions.
falsifiable_prediction: On low-texture regions of multi-view stereo benchmarks with GT geometry, overlapping-stride aggregation of the same frozen backbone will raise reprojection-verified match recall substantially over standard single-stride extraction, at unchanged model weights.
why_important: A zero-training recipe that extends frozen-feature matching into low-texture regions widens where cheap 2D backbones can replace engineered matchers in reconstruction and localization.
why_possibly_novel: Stride-aggregation is known for semantic sharpness, but its effect on low-texture geometric matching measured by reprojection recall appears uncharacterized (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select low-texture regions via local contrast statistics on standard MVS scenes, run matching from single-stride versus shifted-stride-aggregated features, and compare recall at fixed reprojection thresholds and triangulation error of accepted matches.
main_risk: Compute grows with stride density, and aggregation may blur across depth edges, trading one failure for another.
community_default_belief: Textureless regions carry too little photometric signal for passive feature matching, regardless of extraction details.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shading varies smoothly but measurably across most matte surfaces; the signal exists below the patch-grid Nyquist limit and is destroyed by coarse tokenization rather than absent.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 20 low-texture scene pairs, stride-1/4-offset aggregation versus baseline, recall-at-threshold comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if low-texture match recall improves by under 25% relative, or if accepted-match triangulation error worsens by more than 10%.

one_line_idea: Decomposing 2D features into view-invariant and view-dependent components before lifting them into 3D feature fields yields more geometrically faithful fields than the standard practice of averaging raw features across views.
problem: 3D feature fields are built by averaging multi-view 2D features per 3D point, silently mixing view-dependent components (lighting, specular response, occlusion context) into a representation treated as view-invariant.
core_hypothesis: A per-scene low-rank decomposition separating features into a view-independent term plus a small view-conditioned residual will reduce cross-view inconsistency of the lifted field and improve geometry-sensitive downstream readouts without new pretraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Fields built with the decomposition will improve 3D point re-identification accuracy across held-out views and reduce feature-field gradient noise near smooth surfaces, compared to mean-aggregated fields from identical inputs.
why_important: Feature fields are becoming the interface between 2D foundation models and 3D reasoning; a principled aggregation fix improves every consumer of that interface at low cost.
why_possibly_novel: View-dependence-aware aggregation is standard for radiance but appears unexamined for lifted semantic features, where mean pooling remains default (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On multi-view scenes with GT geometry, lift features by (a) per-point mean and (b) low-rank view-decomposed aggregation; evaluate held-out-view point re-identification and consistency of field values at GT-corresponding points.
main_risk: The decomposition may absorb genuine semantic variation into the view-dependent term, diluting semantics; needs a semantic retrieval control.
community_default_belief: Averaging 2D features across registered views is an adequate estimator of a point's canonical descriptor.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Features are trained on single images and demonstrably carry illumination and context signatures; averaging biased samples yields a biased canonical descriptor, especially with few or clustered views.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 5 scenes, rank-1 view-dependent term, held-out-view re-identification delta.
kill_threshold: Kill if held-out-view point re-identification improves by under 5% relative on 4 of 5 scenes.

one_line_idea: Jointly distilling 2D semantic features into Gaussian-splat scenes measurably degrades the recovered geometry relative to photometric-only optimization, a cost the feature-field literature does not report.
problem: Feature-distilled 3D Gaussian scenes are evaluated on semantic utility and rendering quality, while effects on the underlying geometry are rarely quantified.
core_hypothesis: Feature-rendering losses reward placing primitives where 2D features are stable rather than where surfaces are, systematically biasing Gaussian positions and opacities and worsening depth and surface accuracy versus photometric-only baselines.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes with GT geometry, adding standard feature-distillation losses will worsen rendered-depth error and surface chamfer distance relative to photometric-only training at matched primitive budgets and iterations.
why_important: Feature-augmented 3D scenes are being adopted as maps for robotics and AR where geometric accuracy is the point; an unreported geometry tax changes the design tradeoff.
why_possibly_novel: Geometry-side ablations of feature distillation (depth error, chamfer, normal error) appear absent from the feature-field literature, which reports semantic metrics (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train splat scenes with and without feature-distillation losses on scanned scenes with GT meshes, matching primitive counts and schedules; report rendered-depth AbsRel, chamfer distance, and normal angular error.
main_risk: Effect size may depend on loss weighting; requires a weight sweep to distinguish inherent conflict from bad tuning.
community_default_belief: Feature distillation is a free add-on to radiance-field or splat training that leaves geometry unchanged or slightly improves it via extra signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The feature loss is minimized by feature-stable placements, and feature stability correlates with texture, not with true surfaces, in exactly the regions where geometry is hardest.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: 3 scenes with GT meshes, with/without distillation at one weight, chamfer and depth deltas.
kill_threshold: Kill if geometry degradation is under 5% relative on all metrics across the loss-weight sweep, indicating the tax is negligible.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: presence and weight of feature-distillation loss

one_line_idea: Foundation features cannot disambiguate the front and back of near-symmetric objects, and the error direction is predicted by canonical-pose frequency in web imagery, making pose pipelines built on them systematically biased rather than randomly wrong.
problem: Object pose estimation increasingly bootstraps from foundation-feature matching, but symmetry-related failures are treated as noise instead of being characterized.
core_hypothesis: For objects with approximate front-back symmetry, feature matching resolves the ambiguity by defaulting to the pose most frequent in web photos, producing structured 180-degree errors whose frequency tracks canonical-pose bias rather than image evidence.
falsifiable_prediction: On rendered symmetric-object pose tasks, the distribution of 180-degree flip errors will correlate with an independent estimate of view-frequency bias per category, and flips will persist even when disambiguating cues are clearly visible.
why_important: Structured bias is fixable (priors can be subtracted, cues can be reweighted) while random noise is not; robotics grasping and AR anchoring need to know which one they face.
why_possibly_novel: Attributing symmetry-flip statistics to web view-frequency priors, with a quantitative correlation, appears untested (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render pose-estimation probes for symmetric assets with controlled disambiguating cues, run feature-matching-based pose estimation, and correlate flip rates with view-frequency statistics estimated from a public image corpus per category.
main_risk: View-frequency estimation from a corpus is itself noisy; needs a robustness check across corpora.
community_default_belief: Pose errors on symmetric objects are irreducible ambiguity noise inherent to the object, not a model-specific bias.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The models were trained on a heavily biased distribution of object views, and ambiguity resolution under bias defaults to the prior, which is measurable and correctable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 20 categories, rendered flip-rate versus corpus view-frequency correlation.
kill_threshold: Kill if the flip-rate/view-frequency rank correlation is below 0.4, or if visible disambiguating cues reduce flips below 5% (bias absent).

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: object symmetry and visible disambiguating cues

one_line_idea: The believed semantics-versus-geometry fine-tuning tradeoff in foundation backbones is a protocol artifact: tuning only late blocks at small learning rates buys large geometry gains at near-zero semantic cost.
problem: Teams keep backbones frozen for 3D tasks because fine-tuning is believed to catastrophically erode semantic quality, forcing adapter complexity into every 3D pipeline.
core_hypothesis: The reported tradeoff comes from full-network tuning at semantic-task learning rates; geometry-relevant capacity is concentrated in late blocks whose careful tuning improves depth and correspondence probes while leaving semantic retrieval essentially intact.
falsifiable_prediction: A last-25%-of-blocks tuning schedule on a geometry objective will improve depth-probe error and correspondence recall by a large margin over frozen features while semantic retrieval and linear classification drop by only a small margin, across at least two backbone families.
why_important: If true, the field can stop paying the adapter tax and ship single backbones that serve both semantic and geometric consumers.
why_possibly_novel: Block-stratified tuning studies exist for semantics, but a geometry-objective tuning frontier mapped jointly against semantic retention appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep tuned-block fraction and learning rate on a multi-view geometry objective; measure the joint frontier of depth-probe AbsRel, correspondence recall, and semantic retrieval accuracy versus the frozen baseline.
main_risk: The frontier may be data-dependent; requires indoor and outdoor training mixes to check stability.
community_default_belief: Fine-tuning a foundation backbone on geometric objectives destroys its general-purpose semantic value, so freezing is mandatory.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Catastrophic forgetting scales with how much of the network moves; the belief was set by full-tuning experiments and never re-checked with surgical schedules on geometry objectives.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: one backbone, 3 tuned-block fractions, joint geometry/semantic metric table.
kill_threshold: Kill if every schedule that improves depth-probe AbsRel by 15% relative also costs more than 3% absolute semantic retrieval accuracy.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: tuned-block fraction and learning rate under geometry objective

one_line_idea: Monocular depth foundation models infer focal length implicitly from image content, and their metric-depth errors are largely explained by the error of that hidden focal estimate.
problem: Metric monocular depth models are deployed on images with unknown intrinsics, yet their error structure is reported as scene-level statistics with no accounting of the intrinsics-inference component.
core_hypothesis: These models contain an implicit focal-length estimator driven by content cues (face sizes, room proportions, edge convergence), and metric-depth error decomposes into a dominant multiplicative term tracking hidden focal error plus a smaller residual.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-rendering the same scenes at multiple focal lengths will produce depth errors that are predictable from a focal-estimation probe on the model's intermediate features, with the multiplicative error component explaining most of the variance in metric AbsRel across focal conditions.
why_important: If focal inference dominates metric error, supplying or estimating intrinsics separately fixes most of the problem, redirecting effort away from bigger depth decoders.
why_possibly_novel: Decomposing metric-depth error into implicit-focal error plus residual via controlled focal re-rendering appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render or crop-zoom real scenes across a focal sweep with fixed GT depth, evaluate a metric depth model, probe intermediate features for focal estimates, and regress depth error against probed focal error.
main_risk: Crop-zoom changes composition cues as well as intrinsics; needs true re-rendering or careful field-of-view controls.
community_default_belief: Metric depth models learn depth end-to-end, and intrinsics sensitivity is one unstructured error source among many.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Metric depth from a single image is mathematically impossible without an intrinsics assumption, so the model must be making one internally, and internal estimates have measurable, structured errors.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: synthetic focal sweep on 20 scenes, error-versus-focal curve plus feature probe.
kill_threshold: Kill if the focal-linked multiplicative component explains under 30% of metric AbsRel variance across the sweep.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: camera focal length at fixed scene

one_line_idea: Generalization of monocular depth models scales with scene-layout diversity of training data, not raw image count, and layout-diversity-matched subsets can replicate full-data performance at a fraction of the size.
problem: Depth model training mixes keep growing, but there is no controlled account of which data property actually buys cross-domain generalization.
core_hypothesis: Cross-domain depth error is governed by coverage of scene-layout statistics (depth-range distribution, openness, clutter) rather than image count; beyond layout coverage saturation, additional images yield negligible gains.
falsifiable_prediction: Training identical architectures on (a) random subsets and (b) layout-diversity-stratified subsets of the same pool will show the stratified subsets matching full-pool cross-domain AbsRel at severalfold smaller size, while random subsets of equal size lag.
why_important: Data acquisition and licensing dominate the cost of depth foundation models; a validated diversity criterion converts data curation from folklore to measurement.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-specific data-scaling analyses controlling for layout statistics rather than dataset identity appear missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define layout descriptors from GT depth statistics, construct matched-size random versus diversity-stratified training subsets, train identical models, and evaluate on held-out domains.
main_risk: Layout descriptors may miss the true governing property (materials, lighting), yielding a false negative on the specific descriptor set rather than on the diversity thesis.
community_default_belief: More images monotonically improve depth generalization, so scale is the primary lever.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Depth error concentrates on layout regimes absent from training; duplicating well-covered regimes adds nothing, which is invisible in aggregate metrics but decisive under stratified evaluation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three GPU-days: two subset policies at one size on one public pool, cross-domain AbsRel comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if diversity-stratified subsets beat random subsets by under 5% relative cross-domain AbsRel at equal size.

one_line_idea: Teacher-student pseudo-label distillation, the engine of current depth foundation models, systematically erodes depth discontinuities with each generation, measurable as monotonic depth-edge degradation across distillation rounds.
problem: Pseudo-label distillation on unlabeled images is credited for depth generalization gains, with quality reported via global metrics that barely weight discontinuities.
core_hypothesis: Averaging effects in teacher ensembling and student regression act as an edge low-pass filter: each distillation generation smooths depth discontinuities further, degrading edge localization while global AbsRel improves or holds.
falsifiable_prediction: Across successive distillation generations of the same pipeline, depth-boundary localization error on edge-annotated benchmarks will increase monotonically while global AbsRel does not, and the effect will scale with the amount of pseudo-labeled data.
why_important: Edges are what grasping, occlusion reasoning, and compositing consume; a hidden edge tax means the flagship training recipe optimizes the wrong thing for key consumers.
why_possibly_novel: Generation-stratified edge-metric audits of distillation pipelines appear unreported; papers compare endpoint models only (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-run a public distillation recipe for 2-3 generations at reduced scale, evaluating each generation on depth-edge completeness and localization metrics alongside global error on edge-annotated depth data.
main_risk: Small-scale reruns may not reproduce large-scale dynamics; conclusions need a scale-sensitivity caveat.
community_default_belief: Pseudo-label distillation is a near-free way to convert unlabeled images into depth performance, with quality summarized by global error metrics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regression to soft targets provably shrinks high-frequency components under label noise, and depth edges are exactly the high-frequency, high-disagreement pixels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: one distillation generation versus its teacher on an edge-annotated benchmark, edge-localization delta.
kill_threshold: Kill if edge-localization error grows by under 5% relative per generation, or if it improves, across two generations.

one_line_idea: Ordinal errors of relative-depth models concentrate at object-ground contact ambiguities, so a contact-focused probe set exposes large headroom that whole-image ranking metrics hide.
problem: Relative depth is described as essentially solved because whole-image ordinal accuracy is high, yet downstream failures (AR occlusion glitches, wrong support relations) persist.
core_hypothesis: Remaining ordinal errors are not uniformly distributed but concentrate at pixel pairs spanning object-ground contact and support boundaries, where pictorial cues are ambiguous; aggregate ordinal metrics dilute these decisive pairs.
falsifiable_prediction: Constructing pair-sampling protocols focused on contact regions from existing GT depth will show ordinal accuracy dropping far below the whole-image figure for the same state-of-the-art models, with consistent error direction (objects fused to ground).
why_important: Contact relations drive occlusion, support, and physical plausibility reasoning; knowing that they are the residual failure redirects both training data and evaluation design.
why_possibly_novel: Contact-stratified ordinal evaluation of modern relative-depth models appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: From existing RGB-D datasets, sample ordinal pairs stratified as contact-spanning versus generic, evaluate public relative-depth models, and compare stratified ordinal accuracies and error directions.
main_risk: Contact regions have higher GT depth noise in consumer RGB-D data; needs sensor-noise-aware filtering.
community_default_belief: Relative depth ranking is a solved capability, with remaining errors being unstructured residual noise.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Monocular contact cues (shadows, occlusion boundaries) are exactly the cues that web-scale photography renders inconsistent, so models plausibly never learned them reliably; aggregate metrics cannot see it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: 2k contact-spanning pairs from one RGB-D dataset, two public models, stratified ordinal accuracy.
kill_threshold: Kill if contact-stratified ordinal accuracy is within 5 points of generic-pair accuracy for both models.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: ordinal pair sampling stratum (contact vs generic)

one_line_idea: Detected object instances of known physical size classes act as an implicit calibration rig: a post-hoc scale solver over class-size priors converts relative depth to metric depth competitively with intrinsics-aware models on populated scenes.
problem: Metric depth is gated on knowing camera intrinsics or training metric heads per camera family, blocking deployment on arbitrary web and archival imagery.
core_hypothesis: For scenes containing common object classes, a robust joint solve over class-size distributions and a global scale-shift transform yields metric depth whose accuracy approaches intrinsics-conditioned models, because size priors over multiple instances over-constrain the scale.
falsifiable_prediction: On populated indoor and street scenes, prior-solved metric depth from a relative-depth backbone will land within a modest factor of intrinsics-aware baselines in scale-error percentiles, and accuracy will improve predictably with the number of detected known-size instances.
why_important: It unlocks metric 3D from uncalibrated single images at scale, and quantifies exactly when object priors substitute for calibration.
why_possibly_novel: Object-size priors have been used ad hoc; a characterized, uncertainty-weighted solver with instance-count scaling laws appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the solver over public class-size statistics, run on RGB-D scenes stratified by known-size instance count, and report scale-error distribution versus instance count against an intrinsics-aware baseline.
main_risk: Class-size variance (children versus adults, chair types) may leave irreducible scale noise; the scaling curve versus instance count is the diagnostic.
community_default_belief: Metric scale from a single uncalibrated image is unreliable folklore, acceptable only as a rough heuristic.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale error from size priors averages down with independent instances roughly as root-n, so populated scenes can beat the single-cue intuition the folklore is based on.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 100 populated scenes, solver versus GT scale, error-versus-instance-count curve.
kill_threshold: Kill if median absolute scale error exceeds 20% even for scenes with 5+ known-size instances.

one_line_idea: Depth foundation models fail on non-pinhole imagery with a characteristic radial error signature, and a lens-conditioned resampling wrapper recovers most of the loss without retraining the backbone.
problem: Fisheye, action-camera, and panoramic imagery is pervasive, yet depth models are trained and evaluated almost exclusively on near-pinhole projections.
core_hypothesis: On distorted projections these models produce errors that are a deterministic function of radial position (depth bowing tracking local focal-length variation), implying the failure is a projection mismatch rather than a representation gap, and is correctable by projection-aware resampling.
falsifiable_prediction: Error-versus-image-radius curves on real fisheye captures will show a monotone radial bias consistent across scenes and models, and piecewise-pinhole resampling before inference will remove most of the radial component of AbsRel.
why_important: A projection wrapper is orders cheaper than retraining foundation models per lens family, and the radial signature diagnoses when it suffices.
why_possibly_novel: Radius-stratified error decomposition of depth foundation models on real wide-angle lenses, with a resampling-recovery bound, appears unreported (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or reuse calibrated fisheye RGB-D data, evaluate public depth models raw versus after piecewise-pinhole resampling, and report radial error profiles and recovery fractions.
main_risk: Resampling introduces interpolation artifacts and field-of-view seams that may add their own error floor.
community_default_belief: Depth models generalize across cameras, and distortion is a minor preprocessing detail handled by undistortion when intrinsics happen to be known.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The perspective-scale cues these models rely on vary with local focal length across a distorted image, so the failure is structural and spatially systematic, not minor.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one calibrated fisheye RGB-D set, radial error profile raw versus resampled.
kill_threshold: Kill if the radial error component is under 10% of total AbsRel on raw fisheye inputs, meaning the problem is negligible.

one_line_idea: Restricting test-time adaptation of video depth to per-sequence scale-shift-bias parameters under multi-view photometric consistency gives robust cross-domain gains where full-model TTA collapses.
problem: Test-time adaptation for depth is considered unstable because photometric self-supervision at test time can degrade the model catastrophically on hard sequences.
core_hypothesis: Instability comes from adapting high-capacity weights on a biased self-supervised signal; constraining adaptation to a handful of affine parameters per sequence keeps the photometric signal identifiable and converts TTA from risky to reliably positive.
falsifiable_prediction: On cross-domain video sequences with GT depth, affine-only TTA will improve AbsRel on a clear majority of sequences with bounded worst-case degradation, while full-decoder TTA under the identical loss shows heavy-tailed failures.
why_important: A safe TTA recipe converts every deployed depth system into one that self-corrects domain shift without fleet retraining, and the capacity-stability tradeoff generalizes to other dense regressors.
why_possibly_novel: Capacity-stratified stability analysis of photometric TTA (affine versus decoder versus full) with worst-case guarantees appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement photometric-consistency TTA at three capacity tiers on cross-domain driving and handheld sequences, and report per-sequence AbsRel delta distributions including worst-decile behavior.
main_risk: Affine capacity may be too small to fix structured errors (edges, thin objects), capping the achievable gain.
community_default_belief: Test-time photometric adaptation of depth models is too unstable for production use.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The instability evidence conflates adaptation signal quality with adaptation capacity; a 4-parameter update cannot collapse a network and the photometric signal is sufficient to fit 4 parameters.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 30 cross-domain sequences, affine versus full TTA, per-sequence delta histogram.
kill_threshold: Kill if affine-only TTA fails to improve median AbsRel by at least 5% relative, or if its worst-decile degradation exceeds 3% relative.

one_line_idea: A linear readout on frozen self-supervised features already sits within a small margin of specialized depth architectures on standard benchmarks, implying the benchmarks no longer measure depth-decoder research.
problem: Depth papers continue to introduce specialized decoders and losses, evaluated on a handful of standard benchmarks, without a strong frozen-linear baseline to calibrate what the benchmark can still distinguish.
core_hypothesis: Frozen foundation features plus a linear or shallow probe capture most benchmark-measurable depth signal; the residual gap to full systems is smaller than typical inter-paper deltas, meaning benchmark progress mostly re-measures the backbone.
falsifiable_prediction: A careful linear probe on the best frozen backbone will land within a small relative AbsRel margin of recent specialized systems on standard indoor and outdoor benchmarks, and the probe-to-system gap will be smaller than the spread among the systems themselves.
why_important: If the floor is that high, the community should either adopt harder evaluation regimes (edges, thin structures, unusual layouts) or stop attributing benchmark deltas to decoder innovations.
why_possibly_novel: Probe-calibrated benchmark headroom analysis is common in semantics but appears unapplied to depth benchmark culture (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train linear and 2-layer probes on frozen features of 2-3 backbones for standard benchmarks, compare against published system results, and report the probe-to-system gap versus inter-system spread.
main_risk: Probe training details (resolution, loss) can swing results; requires a standardized, well-tuned probe protocol to be fair in both directions.
community_default_belief: Specialized depth decoders and objectives contribute the decisive share of benchmark performance beyond the backbone.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Backbone scale has grown far faster than decoder innovation, and dense probes have historically caught up to specialized heads a few years after each backbone generation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one backbone, tuned linear probe on one benchmark, gap measurement.
kill_threshold: Kill if the best probe remains more than 15% relative AbsRel behind the median recent specialized system on both benchmarks.

one_line_idea: Low-light depth degradation of foundation models is dominated by a structured, exposure-predictable bias rather than variance, so a tiny exposure-conditioned correction head recovers most of the loss without retraining.
problem: Depth models degrade in low light, and the degradation is treated as irreducible noise motivating sensor fusion or heavy retraining.
core_hypothesis: Under low light, depth errors are mostly systematic (global underestimation of range and compression of far-field structure) and predictable from exposure statistics, so a small correction module conditioned on exposure features can restore a large fraction of accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Error decomposition on paired day/night or bracketed-exposure captures will attribute the majority of added AbsRel to a low-dimensional bias field, and a correction head with under 1% of backbone parameters will recover more than half of the low-light degradation.
why_important: Night operation is where depth failures are costly; a near-free correction beats both expensive retraining and added sensors for many applications.
why_possibly_novel: Bias/variance decomposition of low-light depth error with an exposure-conditioned correction bound appears unreported (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use datasets with day/night or exposure-bracketed geometry-paired captures, fit the low-dimensional bias model per condition, train the correction head on one domain, and test recovery on held-out scenes.
main_risk: Sensor noise at extreme darkness may genuinely raise variance, capping recoverable error below the target.
community_default_belief: Low-light depth failure reflects missing information in the image and can only be fixed with better sensors or large-scale night training data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Much of the failure may be a domain-prior mismatch (models calibrated to daytime luminance statistics), which is a correctable bias, not missing information.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: exposure-bracketed set, bias-field fit, fraction-of-error-explained statistic.
kill_threshold: Kill if the structured bias component explains under 40% of low-light AbsRel increase, or the correction head recovers under 30%.

one_line_idea: Small-baseline temporal parallax in casual video contains enough signal to resolve metric scale without IMU or intrinsics, and current video depth models fail to exploit it, as revealed by a parallax-ablation test.
problem: Video depth models are marketed as temporally consistent, but it is unknown whether they actually use inter-frame parallax as a geometric signal or merely smooth per-frame predictions.
core_hypothesis: Handheld jitter provides usable metric parallax; models trained with explicit multi-frame geometric losses can recover absolute scale from it, while current systems show near-zero sensitivity to parallax ablation, proving they ignore the signal.
falsifiable_prediction: Synthetically freezing camera translation (temporal replication with matched noise) will leave current video-depth outputs nearly unchanged, while a parallax-aware model will degrade on scale metrics when parallax is removed and beat single-frame baselines on metric error when it is present.
why_important: Free metric scale from casual video would remove the calibration bottleneck for consumer 3D applications; the ablation also gives the field a clean test of whether temporal models do geometry or smoothing.
why_possibly_novel: The parallax-ablation sensitivity test as a published diagnostic, and a metric-from-jitter capability claim quantified against it, appear new (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate public video-depth models on sequences with GT metric depth under real versus parallax-ablated inputs; train a small multi-frame model with an explicit two-view metric loss and compare scale-error sensitivity.
main_risk: Rolling-shutter and motion blur may corrupt the tiny-baseline signal below usability on real footage.
community_default_belief: Casual handheld video lacks sufficient baseline for metric depth, so scale must come from IMU, intrinsics, or learned priors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Centimeter-level jitter at typical scene depths yields parallax well above modern sub-pixel matching accuracy, so the information is present and simply unexploited.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: parallax-ablation sensitivity of two public video-depth models on 20 GT sequences.
kill_threshold: Kill the capability claim if the parallax-aware prototype reduces median scale error by under 20% relative to its single-frame twin on jittery sequences.

one_line_idea: Ad hoc sky handling in depth training pipelines systematically distorts far-field geometry and horizon placement, and the distortion is measurable and correctable with a principled at-infinity parameterization.
problem: Sky pixels are handled by heuristics (fixed large constants, exclusion, clamping) that differ across pipelines, and nobody quantifies how these choices propagate into near-horizon geometry.
core_hypothesis: Heuristic sky treatment biases the regression targets adjacent to the horizon, causing systematic overestimation compression of far-field depth and horizon-height errors, with the bias signature differing predictably by sky-handling scheme.
falsifiable_prediction: Models trained identically except for sky-handling scheme will show divergent error profiles in the top far-field depth decile and different horizon-line estimates, while mid-range metrics stay indistinguishable; a disparity-at-infinity parameterization will show the flattest far-field bias.
why_important: Far-field geometry drives planning horizons in driving and drone autonomy; a pipeline-choice artifact that shifts the horizon is a silent safety issue and an easy fix.
why_possibly_novel: Controlled comparison of sky-handling schemes with far-field-stratified and horizon metrics appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models on outdoor data under 3 sky-handling schemes, evaluate far-field-stratified depth error and horizon estimation on held-out scenes with GT geometry.
main_risk: Far-field GT itself is noisy in most datasets; requires careful choice of supervision with reliable long-range measurements.
community_default_belief: Sky handling is an implementation detail with no bearing on the geometry of actual scene content.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regression networks smooth across label discontinuities, so an arbitrary sky constant necessarily leaks into adjacent far-field predictions; the only question is magnitude.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: two schemes, one outdoor dataset, far-field decile error comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if far-field decile AbsRel differs by under 5% relative across schemes, showing the artifact is negligible.

one_line_idea: Depth foundation models are substantially worse in the near-field manipulation zone (under 1 meter) than benchmark averages imply, because standard benchmarks under-sample exactly that range.
problem: Robotic manipulation consumes depth in the 0.1-1 meter range, but flagship depth benchmarks are dominated by room-scale and street-scale content, and published averages are read as general competence.
core_hypothesis: Training and evaluation range distributions under-represent near-field geometry, so relative error in the manipulation zone is a multiple of the benchmark average, with characteristic failures on foreshortening and defocus that range-stratified evaluation will expose.
falsifiable_prediction: Range-stratified evaluation on existing close-range RGB-D captures will show near-field relative error substantially exceeding the same models' mid-range error, and the gap will shrink for models whose training mixes include close-range data, tracing the failure to data coverage.
why_important: Depth-model claims are increasingly cited in robotics stacks; a range-stratified truth-in-advertising result redirects both dataset construction and model choice for manipulation.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic near-field stratification of depth foundation models against training-range statistics appears unreported (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble close-range evaluation splits from existing RGB-D sources, evaluate public models with range-stratified AbsRel and delta thresholds, and correlate near-field performance with documented training-range coverage.
main_risk: Consumer RGB-D ground truth has its own close-range error profile; needs sensor-error modeling or higher-grade GT subsets.
community_default_belief: A depth model that excels on standard benchmarks is presumed accurate across the whole practical range, including close-up.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Error statistics are dominated by the range regimes the data contains, and close-range optics (defocus, strong perspective) differ qualitatively from the room-scale regime the models mastered.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: two public models on one close-range RGB-D set, near-field versus mid-range stratified error.
kill_threshold: Kill if near-field AbsRel exceeds mid-range AbsRel by under 30% relative for most tested models.

one_line_idea: Optical flow benchmarks hide an unsolved motion-blur regime: blur-stratified evaluation will show error concentrating on high-blur pixels, where current models degrade to near-uselessness while averages look solved.
problem: Flow benchmark averages have plateaued at low error, driving a solved-problem narrative, but per-pixel error is never reported as a function of local motion blur magnitude.
core_hypothesis: Fast motion produces blur that destroys the local evidence current matching-based architectures rely on; blur-stratified end-point error will reveal a severe unsolved regime invisible in aggregate statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: On benchmarks with known GT motion, end-point error in the top blur decile will exceed the dataset average by a large multiple for all leading models, and ranking among models will differ between blur strata and the aggregate.
why_important: High-speed motion is precisely where downstream consumers (collision prediction, sports analysis, robotics) most need flow; a hidden regime failure redefines what flow progress means.
why_possibly_novel: Blur-magnitude stratification as a standard reporting axis for flow appears absent from benchmark culture (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate per-pixel blur from GT motion and exposure assumptions on synthetic benchmarks, stratify end-point error by blur decile for several public models, and compare stratum rankings to aggregate rankings.
main_risk: Synthetic blur models may not match real camera blur; needs a real high-speed-camera control subset.
community_default_belief: Optical flow is essentially solved, with remaining benchmark error attributed to occlusions and fine structures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The evidence for solved status comes from averages over datasets whose blur distribution is mild; correlation-based matching provably degrades as blur suppresses distinctive local structure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one synthetic benchmark with motion-derived blur estimates, two models, top-decile versus average end-point error.
kill_threshold: Kill if top-blur-decile end-point error is under 2x the dataset average for the leading models.

one_line_idea: Iterative recurrent refinement in flow architectures is largely an inference-time crutch: a single-pass global-matching model with a strong upsampler can match refinement-based accuracy at a fraction of latency on high-resolution video.
problem: The dominant flow architecture family spends most of its latency on recurrent refinement iterations, which is a major obstacle for real-time high-resolution deployment.
core_hypothesis: Refinement iterations mainly correct upsampling and initialization artifacts rather than performing essential inference, so investing the same compute in one-shot global matching plus a learned high-fidelity upsampling head reaches equal accuracy at much lower latency.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched training data and parameter budget, the one-shot design will reach within a small end-point-error margin of the recurrent baseline on standard benchmarks while cutting high-resolution latency severalfold, and the recurrent model's per-iteration gains will be shown to concentrate in regions of poor initialization.
why_important: Flow is a building block for video editing, robotics, and world models; removing the iteration tax makes dense motion affordable at production resolutions.
why_possibly_novel: One-shot flow exists, but a controlled iteration-value decomposition showing where refinement helps, tied to an equal-budget one-shot design, appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched one-shot and recurrent models on identical data; report accuracy-latency curves at multiple resolutions and a per-iteration error-reduction decomposition by region type for the recurrent model.
main_risk: Large displacements with repetitive texture may genuinely need iterative disambiguation, capping one-shot accuracy on hard subsets.
community_default_belief: Recurrent refinement is the essential ingredient of accurate optical flow and cannot be removed without large accuracy loss.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The belief was set when global matching was weak; modern attention-based matching resolves most ambiguity in one pass, leaving iterations to polish details a better upsampler could handle.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: fine-tune an existing global-matching model with an upgraded upsampling head, compare against a recurrent baseline at matched data on one benchmark with latency profiling.
kill_threshold: Kill if the one-shot design remains over 10% relative end-point error behind at under 2x speedup on high-resolution inputs.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: refinement iterations vs one-shot matching budget

one_line_idea: Flow models track texture translation, not motion: on isoluminant color motion and other texture-decoupled stimuli they will fail catastrophically, exposing that learned flow lacks the motion-energy computation biological vision has.
problem: Learned flow models are described as motion estimators, but their training pairs conflate motion with texture displacement, and no benchmark separates the two.
core_hypothesis: Current models compute displacement of luminance texture; when motion is carried by chromatic contrast, contrast-envelope drift, or other second-order signals that humans perceive, learned models will report near-zero or wrong flow.
falsifiable_prediction: On procedurally generated isoluminant and second-order motion stimuli with exact GT, leading flow models will show end-point error an order of magnitude above their natural-scene error, while a model given a motion-energy front end recovers much of it.
why_important: It defines what current flow actually measures, predicts failure niches in natural footage (shadow motion, specular sweep, biological motion at low contrast), and motivates front-end designs beyond raw-frame correlation.
why_possibly_novel: Psychophysics-style second-order motion probes applied systematically to modern learned flow appear unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate luminance-matched chromatic-motion and contrast-modulated stimuli with GT flow, evaluate public models, and compare error to matched luminance-texture controls.
main_risk: Isoluminant stimuli are out-of-distribution in low-level statistics beyond motion content, so controls must equate everything except the motion carrier.
community_default_belief: Learned flow generalizes across motion types because it learned motion, not appearance displacement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in the training distribution or architecture rewards sensitivity to non-luminance motion carriers, so the capability has no reason to exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: 200 procedural stimuli, two models, error ratio to luminance controls.
kill_threshold: Kill if end-point error on texture-decoupled stimuli is under 3x the matched luminance-control error, indicating models do handle second-order motion.

one_line_idea: On mostly-static scenes, point-tracking benchmark performance is largely explained by camera-geometry propagation, so learned trackers should be credited only for their margin over a depth-plus-pose geometric baseline.
problem: Point trackers are evaluated on benchmarks mixing camera-induced and object-induced motion, and headline numbers are attributed to learned tracking ability.
core_hypothesis: For static-scene content, propagating points through estimated depth and camera pose reproduces most of the benchmark score; the learned tracker's real contribution concentrates on dynamic objects and occlusions, a much smaller pixel fraction than the metrics imply.
falsifiable_prediction: A no-learning-at-track-time baseline (frozen depth and pose estimators plus reprojection) will reach a large fraction of learned-tracker position accuracy on static-scene subsets, and the learned-versus-geometric gap will concentrate in dynamic-object and occlusion strata.
why_important: Attribution matters for research direction: if geometry explains most of the score, tracking research should target the dynamic residual instead of re-solving camera motion implicitly.
why_possibly_novel: A geometric-propagation control baseline for point-tracking benchmarks, with static/dynamic attribution decomposition, appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Split benchmark sequences into static and dynamic strata using GT or annotation metadata, run the geometric baseline and public trackers, and report stratified position-accuracy and occlusion-handling metrics.
main_risk: Depth and pose estimator errors compound; a weak geometric baseline would understate the geometric share, so components must be state of the art.
community_default_belief: Point-tracking benchmark scores measure learned spatiotemporal correspondence ability end to end.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most pixels in most benchmark videos are static-world points whose image motion is fully determined by camera geometry that modern estimators recover well.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: geometric baseline on the static stratum of one benchmark versus a public tracker.
kill_threshold: Kill if the geometric baseline reaches under 60% of learned-tracker position accuracy on static strata.

one_line_idea: Long-horizon point-tracking failures are dominated by re-identification errors after occlusion, not accumulated drift, so drift-focused architectural work targets the wrong failure mode.
problem: Long-video tracking error is commonly narrated as drift accumulation, motivating ever-longer temporal windows, but no published decomposition separates drift from re-identification failures at occlusion events.
core_hypothesis: Between occlusions, modern trackers drift negligibly; the bulk of long-horizon error arises at reappearance events where the tracker locks onto the wrong location, an error that is categorical rather than accumulative.
falsifiable_prediction: An event-based decomposition on long synthetic sequences with exact GT will attribute the majority of final position error to reappearance mislocks, with inter-occlusion drift contributing a small, sublinear share.
why_important: The fix for drift (longer memory, better integration) differs completely from the fix for re-identification (distinctive descriptors, multi-hypothesis reasoning); the field should know which problem it has.
why_possibly_novel: Event-level error decomposition protocols for long-range tracking appear missing; benchmarks report endpoint statistics only (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On long procedurally generated sequences with occlusion annotations, segment each track into drift phases and reappearance events, and attribute final error to each phase type across public trackers.
main_risk: Synthetic occlusion statistics may not represent real footage; needs a real annotated subset for confirmation.
community_default_belief: Long-range tracking degrades primarily through gradual drift that accumulates over time.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Matching within visible spans is a locally well-posed problem modern models handle; the ill-posed step is discrete re-association, and discrete errors dominate whenever they occur at all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 50 long synthetic sequences, one tracker, error attribution by phase.
kill_threshold: Kill if reappearance events account for under 50% of final-frame position error across trackers.

one_line_idea: Epipolar-constrained self-supervision on unlabeled real video can close most of the synthetic-to-real gap in optical flow, ending the field's structural dependence on synthetic training data.
problem: Flow training remains anchored to synthetic datasets because real GT flow is nearly impossible to capture, leaving a persistent domain gap on real footage.
core_hypothesis: For the static-scene majority of pixels, two-view geometry supplies an exact one-dimensional constraint (flow must lie on the epipolar line given estimated pose); training with this constraint plus photometric consistency and dynamic-region exclusion by residual analysis provides supervision strong enough to fine-tune synthetic-pretrained models into the real domain.
falsifiable_prediction: Epipolar-constrained fine-tuning on unlabeled real video will improve real-benchmark flow error substantially over the synthetic-only baseline and over photometric-only self-supervision, approaching the gain that labeled real data would provide where such proxies exist.
why_important: It converts every hour of real video into flow supervision, removing the biggest structural weakness of the field and enabling domain-targeted flow systems.
why_possibly_novel: Epipolar losses exist in self-supervised depth-pose work, but a systematic flow-centric formulation with residual-based dynamic-region exclusion and a measured share of the synthetic-to-real gap closed appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune a public flow model with the constrained objective on unlabeled driving and handheld video, evaluate on real benchmarks with GT, ablating epipolar versus photometric terms.
main_risk: Pose estimation errors inject correlated noise into the constraint; degenerate motions (pure rotation) give no signal and must be detected.
community_default_belief: Real-world flow supervision at scale is unavailable, so progress must come from better synthetic data and architectures.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The one-dimensional epipolar constraint on the static majority of pixels is exact and free; the community discounts partial supervision because benchmarks reward dense labels, not because the signal is weak.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: constrained fine-tuning on one unlabeled domain, real-benchmark delta versus photometric-only control.
kill_threshold: Kill if constrained fine-tuning improves real-domain end-point error by under 10% relative over the synthetic-only baseline, or fails to beat photometric-only self-supervision.

one_line_idea: Scalar end-point error hides direction errors that dominate downstream time-to-contact and steering computations, and a direction-magnitude decomposed evaluation reorders the flow leaderboard for safety-relevant use.
problem: End-point error is the near-universal flow metric, yet downstream consumers like time-to-contact estimation are far more sensitive to flow direction near the focus of expansion than to magnitude.
core_hypothesis: Models with similar end-point error differ widely in angular error distribution in the regions that matter for egomotion tasks, so leaderboard order does not predict downstream utility; a mechanism-level cause is that training losses penalize magnitude-weighted error, under-weighting slow-moving but direction-critical pixels.
falsifiable_prediction: Recomputing rankings under angular error stratified by distance to the focus of expansion, and under a derived time-to-contact error, will flip model orderings relative to end-point error, with rank correlation clearly below 1 across public models.
why_important: Flow feeds control loops; choosing models by a metric misaligned with control-relevant error can select worse systems while the community believes progress is monotone.
why_possibly_novel: Task-derived error functionals (time-to-contact, divergence) as flow evaluation axes with documented rank instability appear unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For public models on standard benchmarks with egomotion metadata, compute end-point, angular-stratified, and time-to-contact errors, and report cross-metric rank correlations and per-region breakdowns.
main_risk: Time-to-contact derivation amplifies noise near the focus of expansion; estimators must be regularized identically across models.
community_default_belief: End-point error is an adequate single figure of merit for optical flow quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A scalar average cannot represent error anisotropy, and the anisotropy is exactly what downstream geometric computations differentiate on.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: three models, one benchmark, end-point versus angular-stratified rank comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if rank correlation between end-point error and time-to-contact error orderings exceeds 0.9 across at least 6 models, showing the metrics agree in practice.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: error functional (endpoint vs angular vs time-to-contact)

one_line_idea: Explicit multi-hypothesis track states with a lightweight reappearance detector can match heavyweight learned-memory trackers on occlusion recovery at a fraction of compute, showing occlusion handling is a state-representation problem, not a capacity problem.
problem: Occlusion recovery in point tracking is pursued through ever-larger learned memories and attention windows, at growing inference cost.
core_hypothesis: The essential requirement is representational: maintaining a small set of weighted location hypotheses through occlusion plus a discriminative reappearance test; given that state structure, a small model matches large-memory trackers on recovery accuracy because the hard part is not remembering appearance but representing multimodal position uncertainty.
falsifiable_prediction: A tracker with k-hypothesis state (k around 4) and a compact descriptor test will match learned-memory baselines on post-occlusion recovery position accuracy on standard tracking benchmarks while using several times less inference compute.
why_important: If a cheap structured state closes the occlusion gap, long-video tracking becomes affordable on edge devices and the field learns which component actually carries the capability.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-hypothesis filtering is classical, but a controlled capability-attribution study against modern learned-memory trackers on occlusion recovery appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the multi-hypothesis head on a frozen matching backbone, evaluate post-occlusion recovery stratified by occlusion duration against public trackers at matched backbones, with compute profiling.
main_risk: Long occlusions with appearance change may genuinely need rich memory, limiting the parity claim to short and medium occlusions.
community_default_belief: Robust occlusion handling emerges from large learned spatiotemporal memories and cannot be replicated by simple structured states.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Published ablations rarely isolate the memory's role in recovery specifically; multimodal position uncertainty is the textbook failure of unimodal regression and the textbook fix is hypothesis maintenance, not capacity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: prototype head on one benchmark, occlusion-duration-stratified recovery comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if the multi-hypothesis tracker recovers under 80% of the learned-memory baseline's post-occlusion position accuracy on medium occlusions (0.5-2 seconds).

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: track state structure (multi-hypothesis vs learned memory)

one_line_idea: Monocular feed-forward 4D reconstruction now implies scene flow good enough to rival LiDAR-supervised methods for medium-range dynamics, collapsing a sensor requirement into a software capability.
problem: Scene flow (3D motion fields) is treated as requiring LiDAR or stereo rigs for both training and inference, restricting it to instrumented platforms.
core_hypothesis: Chaining dynamic-aware monocular reconstruction with temporal point correspondence yields metric 3D motion fields whose medium-range accuracy approaches LiDAR-supervised scene flow, because the binding constraint was geometry quality, which foundation reconstructors have largely fixed.
falsifiable_prediction: On driving benchmarks with LiDAR-derived GT dynamics, the monocular pipeline will reach a substantial fraction of LiDAR-supervised 3D end-point-error performance within 30 meters, degrading predictably with range, and will beat classical monocular baselines by a wide margin.
why_important: Scene flow from a single camera turns every dashcam and drone into a 3D dynamics sensor, changing data economics for autonomy and world-model training.
why_possibly_novel: Quantified parity analysis of monocular-reconstruction-based scene flow against LiDAR-supervised systems, with range-stratified error, appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compose public monocular 4D reconstruction and tracking components, evaluate 3D end-point error on scene-flow-annotated driving data stratified by range, against published LiDAR-supervised references under matched protocols.
main_risk: Metric scale errors from monocular reconstruction multiply into motion error; scale-drift correction may be the real bottleneck.
community_default_belief: Reliable 3D motion estimation requires range sensors; monocular scene flow is a research curiosity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The belief predates feed-forward metric reconstructors; once per-frame geometry is metrically accurate, scene flow reduces to correspondence, which monocular systems already do well.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: composed pipeline on one annotated driving set, range-stratified 3D end-point error versus published reference numbers under matched evaluation.
kill_threshold: Kill if monocular 3D end-point error within 30 meters exceeds 2x the LiDAR-supervised reference on the same scenes.

one_line_idea: Flow models carry a resolution-specific motion prior: evaluated off their training resolution they systematically underestimate large motions in a way predictable from correlation-volume truncation, not random degradation.
problem: Practitioners run flow models at whatever resolution their pipeline uses, assuming mild, unstructured degradation away from training resolution.
core_hypothesis: Displacement priors are baked in pixel units: at higher inference resolution the same physical motion becomes more pixels, exceeding the effective search range set by correlation-volume truncation and learned displacement statistics, producing systematic magnitude underestimation with a predictable onset.
falsifiable_prediction: Error-versus-GT-magnitude curves across inference resolutions will show underestimation onset shifting proportionally with resolution scale factor, matching the effective search range, consistently across architectures with truncated correlation volumes.
why_important: It converts a mysterious deployment failure into a computable operating envelope, and motivates resolution-equivariant motion encodings.
why_possibly_novel: Attributing cross-resolution flow failure specifically to search-range truncation with a quantitative onset prediction appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate public models on the same physical sequences rendered at several resolutions, plot signed magnitude error versus GT displacement per resolution, and compare onset points to architectural search ranges.
