main_risk: Anti-aliasing and detail changes across renders confound with pure resolution effects; needs careful downsampling-chain controls.
community_default_belief: Flow models are approximately resolution-agnostic after standard image rescaling at inference.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both the correlation-volume geometry and the training displacement histogram are defined in pixels, so nothing in the model can be resolution-invariant for large motions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one model, three resolutions, signed-error-versus-magnitude curves.
kill_threshold: Kill if underestimation onset does not shift with resolution (onset ratio within 20% of constant across a 2x resolution change).

one_line_idea: Point trackers trained on rigid-dominated data fail on non-rigid shear and stretching in a structured way: they snap to texture landmarks and refuse continuous deformation, measurable on procedurally deformed surfaces.
problem: Tracking-any-point systems are marketed for arbitrary content, including cloth, tissue, and fluid-like surfaces, but training data motion statistics are dominated by rigid and articulated motion.
core_hypothesis: Under large non-rigid shear, trackers exhibit landmark capture: predictions cluster on distinctive texture points and systematically lag the true continuously deforming correspondence, an error signature distinct from random failure and diagnostic of a rigid-motion prior.
falsifiable_prediction: On simulation-rendered deforming surfaces with exact GT, tracking error will grow superlinearly with local shear magnitude, and error vectors will point toward nearest high-saliency texture landmarks significantly above chance.
why_important: Surgical guidance, cloth manipulation, and soft-body perception need deformation-faithful tracking; a diagnosed prior enables targeted training-data interventions rather than blind scaling.
why_possibly_novel: Shear-stratified evaluation with a landmark-capture statistical test appears absent from the tracking literature (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use physics-based simulation to render deforming textured surfaces with GT correspondence, evaluate public trackers, and test the landmark-attraction hypothesis via error-vector analysis stratified by shear.
main_risk: Rendered deformation may miss real material appearance effects; a small real deformable set with fiducials is the confirmatory step.
community_default_belief: Modern point trackers handle arbitrary deformation as a byproduct of large-scale training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The training distribution shapes the motion prior, and non-rigid shear is rare in it; interpolation cannot supply a deformation model that was never observed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 50 simulated deforming sequences, one tracker, error-versus-shear curve and landmark-attraction test.
kill_threshold: Kill if error grows at most linearly with shear and landmark-attraction is indistinguishable from chance.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: local shear magnitude of surface deformation

one_line_idea: Temporal context beyond two frames pays for itself almost entirely inside occluded regions: multi-frame flow gains are an occlusion-inpainting effect, and reporting occluded/visible strata separately will prove it and redirect multi-frame architecture design.
problem: Multi-frame flow models report modest average gains over two-frame baselines, leaving unclear what the extra frames actually contribute and whether the architecture exploits them well.
core_hypothesis: For visible pixels, two frames are nearly sufficient and extra context adds noise-averaging at best; for occluded pixels, extra frames enable motion extrapolation and reappearance evidence, so nearly all multi-frame improvement concentrates in the occluded stratum.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratified evaluation will show multi-frame gains in occluded-region end-point error several times larger in relative terms than in visible regions, and increasing context from 2 to 5-plus frames will move occluded-region error while visible-region error saturates.
why_important: It tells architects to spend capacity on occlusion-specific temporal reasoning (trajectory models, visibility gating) instead of uniform temporal attention, and gives evaluators the right reporting axis.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion-stratified attribution of multi-frame flow gains across context lengths appears unpublished as a systematic study (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or evaluate matched models at context lengths 2, 3, 5, 8 on benchmarks with occlusion annotations, and report visible/occluded stratified end-point error versus context length.
main_risk: Occlusion annotations differ in definition across benchmarks; the stratification protocol must be fixed and audited first.
community_default_belief: More temporal context helps flow generally and uniformly across the image.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Visible-pixel flow is locally well-posed from two frames, so information-theoretic headroom for extra frames exists only where two-frame evidence is missing, which is precisely occlusion.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one public multi-frame model versus two-frame baseline, occlusion-stratified errors on one benchmark.
kill_threshold: Kill if occluded-region relative gain is under 1.5x the visible-region relative gain, showing gains are not occlusion-concentrated.

one_line_idea: Densify-and-split in Gaussian splatting is an implicit coarse-to-fine annealing schedule, and its scheduling, not the adaptive heuristics, carries most of the quality, testable by matched-budget schedule ablations.
problem: Adaptive densification heuristics are treated as essential, gradient-informed intelligence of splat training, but no study separates their adaptivity from the coarse-to-fine capacity schedule they implement.
core_hypothesis: The quality benefit comes from growing capacity gradually (an optimization annealing effect that avoids early overfitting to sparse view constraints), so a blind capacity schedule that adds primitives at random surface-plausible locations on the same timetable will match adaptive heuristics at equal final primitive count.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched final primitive counts and iteration budgets, blind-schedule training will land within a small margin of adaptive densification on held-out-view reconstruction quality across standard scenes, while single-shot full-capacity initialization will lag both.
why_important: If scheduling is the active ingredient, splat training can be simplified, parallelized, and theoretically analyzed as annealed capacity growth, and heuristic tuning can stop.
why_possibly_novel: Decomposing densification into adaptivity versus scheduling with matched-budget controls appears untested (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement blind capacity-growth schedules with random and depth-guided placement, train on standard multi-view scenes at matched budgets, and compare held-out-view quality and surface accuracy against adaptive baselines and full-capacity-from-start controls.
main_risk: Blind placement may waste capacity in empty space without opacity-based pruning; pruning policy must be equalized across arms.
community_default_belief: Gradient-driven adaptive densification is the key mechanism that makes splat optimization work.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Curriculum effects are notoriously mistaken for mechanism intelligence across machine learning; the heuristic's timing and the capacity curve are perfectly confounded in all published ablations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 3 scenes, blind schedule versus adaptive at matched counts, held-out-view quality deltas.
kill_threshold: Kill if blind schedules lag adaptive densification by more than 1 dB PSNR or 10% relative surface chamfer at matched budgets across most scenes.

one_line_idea: Spherical-harmonic color in Gaussian splatting mostly compensates residual geometric error rather than modeling reflectance: fixing geometry with ground truth collapses the benefit of higher SH orders.
problem: View-dependent color via spherical harmonics is interpreted as capturing material appearance, motivating higher orders and reflectance-oriented extensions.
core_hypothesis: With imperfect primitive geometry, view-dependent color terms act as error absorbers that repaint view-specific misprojections; their contribution tracks geometric error, not material properties, so improving geometry should shrink the SH benefit sharply.
falsifiable_prediction: On scenes with GT geometry, splats initialized and constrained to accurate surfaces will show a much smaller quality gap between low and high SH orders than free-geometry training, and the per-scene SH benefit will correlate with residual geometric error rather than with material glossiness.
why_important: It reframes what appearance capacity is for, cautions against interpreting SH coefficients as reflectance, and suggests geometry investment beats appearance capacity for faithful scene capture.
why_possibly_novel: Decoupling error-absorption from reflectance roles of view-dependent color via GT-geometry controls appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train splats with free versus GT-constrained geometry across SH orders on scanned scenes spanning matte to glossy materials, and regress SH benefit against residual geometric error and material class.
main_risk: GT-constrained optimization may be handicapped in other ways, exaggerating the collapse; constraint strength needs a sweep.
community_default_belief: Higher-order view-dependent color primarily captures real material appearance effects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: An optimizer will use any available capacity to reduce loss, and view-conditioned color is the cheapest way to hide view-specific geometric misprojection; matte scenes benefiting from SH would be the tell.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 3 matte scanned scenes, SH-order sweep under free versus constrained geometry.
kill_threshold: Kill if high-order SH retains over 70% of its quality benefit under GT-constrained geometry on matte scenes.

one_line_idea: Beyond a scene-dependent primitive budget, additional Gaussians fit view-sampling noise: interpolated-view metrics keep improving while extrapolated-view quality degrades, an overfitting signature current protocols never measure.
problem: Splat scenes are trained and evaluated on views drawn from the same camera trajectory distribution, and primitive counts keep growing under the assumption that more capacity is at worst neutral.
core_hypothesis: Excess primitives encode trajectory-specific photometric noise (exposure flicker, motion blur, misregistration), which improves interpolation metrics but actively harms rendering from genuinely novel viewpoints, making primitive count a classic capacity-overfitting axis.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping primitive budgets will show monotone interpolated-view gains but an inverted-U for extrapolated-view quality (held-out orbital or elevated cameras), with the peak shifting earlier for scenes captured with noisier trajectories.
why_important: Robotics and AR consume splat scenes from viewpoints far off the capture path; an unmeasured extrapolation tax means deployed quality is worse than every published number suggests.
why_possibly_novel: Extrapolation-stratified capacity sweeps for splatting appear unpublished; existing protocols hold out interpolating frames only (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On scenes with dense hemispherical captures, train at several primitive budgets using only a trajectory subset, and evaluate quality separately on interpolating versus extrapolating held-out cameras.
main_risk: Extrapolation quality depends on capture coverage; scene selection must vary coverage to avoid confounding budget with visibility.
community_default_belief: More Gaussians monotonically improve or saturate reconstruction quality; capacity control is a memory concern, not a quality concern.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-view photometric nuisances are view-correlated noise, and a representation with millions of free primitives will absorb them exactly as any overparameterized regressor absorbs label noise.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one hemispherical-capture scene, three budgets, interpolation versus extrapolation quality curves.
kill_threshold: Kill if extrapolated-view quality is monotone non-decreasing in primitive budget across scenes (no inverted-U), matching the community belief.

one_line_idea: With opacity-entropy and surface-concentration regularization, splat scenes can serve as measurement-grade geometry, closing most of the surface-accuracy gap to multi-view-stereo pipelines while keeping real-time rendering.
problem: Splatting is treated as a rendering representation whose geometry is decorative, forcing teams that need surfaces to run separate photogrammetry pipelines.
core_hypothesis: The surface-accuracy gap comes from opacity spread and free-floating primitives, both controllable with regularizers that concentrate opacity mass near a 2D manifold; regularized training recovers most of the gap to dedicated MVS on standard geometry benchmarks without sacrificing rendering quality beyond a small margin.
falsifiable_prediction: On MVS benchmarks with GT scans, regularized splat surface extraction will close at least half of the chamfer-distance gap between vanilla splatting and reference MVS pipelines, at under 1 dB rendering-quality cost.
why_important: One representation serving both rendering and metrology removes a whole pipeline stage for scanning, AR anchoring, and inspection applications.
why_possibly_novel: Surface-oriented splat variants exist; a quantified gap-closure claim against MVS references at matched rendering budgets, with the opacity-concentration mechanism isolated by ablation, appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train splats with and without the regularizer suite on scanned-GT benchmarks, extract surfaces by density thresholding plus meshing, and report chamfer and completeness against an MVS reference plus rendering-quality deltas.
main_risk: Regularization may fight view-dependent appearance on glossy scenes, showing up as rendering-quality loss above the budget.
community_default_belief: Splat geometry is intrinsically too diffuse for metrology; serious surface work requires MVS or neural SDF pipelines.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Diffuseness is an artifact of the photometric objective having no reason to concentrate opacity, not of the representation; explicit pressure toward surface concentration changes the optimum.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 3 benchmark scenes, regularized versus vanilla, chamfer gap-closure fraction.
kill_threshold: Kill if gap closure is under 30% on the geometry benchmark or rendering cost exceeds 2 dB.

one_line_idea: Anti-aliasing filters in splatting can be replaced by letting each primitive learn its own scale-space response, removing hand-derived filter approximations and their failure cases at extreme zoom.
problem: Aliasing under zoom and resolution change is handled by analytically derived per-primitive filtering approximations, which embed specific assumptions about the render kernel and break in corner cases.
core_hypothesis: A small learned per-primitive parameterization of appearance versus rendered footprint (a learned scale-space curve per Gaussian) can be optimized jointly with the scene and will match or beat analytic filters across zoom ranges, because the correct filter depends on scene content the analytic derivation ignores.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-scale benchmark protocols, learned scale-response splats will match analytic-filter baselines at moderate zoom and beat them at extreme zoom-out factors by a visible-quality and PSNR margin, with negligible rendering-cost increase.
why_important: Scale robustness is a gating requirement for maps and digital twins viewed at arbitrary distances, and a learned mechanism removes a whole class of derivation-mismatch bugs.
why_possibly_novel: Treating anti-aliasing as a per-primitive learned degree of freedom rather than a fixed analytic correction appears unexplored (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Add a compact per-primitive scale-response parameterization to a public splat implementation, train on multi-scale captures, and evaluate the standard multi-scale protocol against analytic-filter baselines at matched budgets.
main_risk: Extra per-primitive parameters increase memory and may overfit the training zoom range, failing on unseen scales.
community_default_belief: Correct anti-aliasing must be derived analytically from the projection and kernel model; learning it is redundant at best.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The analytic derivation optimizes a proxy (band-limiting an idealized kernel), while the actual objective is perceptual fidelity of a discrete approximation over real content, which a learned response can target directly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one scene family, learned response versus analytic filter across 4 zoom factors.
kill_threshold: Kill if learned responses fail to match analytic filters within 0.3 dB at moderate zoom or to beat them at 8x zoom-out.

one_line_idea: Splatting failures on mirror-like surfaces are optimization pathologies, not representational limits: with reflection-consistent initialization the standard representation converges to virtual-image geometry that renders correctly from held-out views.
problem: Mirror-like view-dependent appearance breaks standard splat training, and the failure is broadly attributed to the representation lacking reflectance physics.
core_hypothesis: The photometric objective admits a good solution in which reflective surfaces are represented via virtual-image primitives behind the mirror plane; standard training misses it due to bad initialization and densification dynamics, not because the solution space lacks it.
falsifiable_prediction: Initializing primitives at mirror-plane-reflected positions (estimated from a coarse plane fit) will let vanilla splat optimization reach large held-out-view quality gains on reflective regions without any change to the representation or renderer, closing much of the gap to reflection-specialized methods.
why_important: Knowing whether failures are optimization or representation determines whether the field needs physics-based extensions or better optimization schedules, a fork worth resolving before more architecture work accumulates.
why_possibly_novel: Reflection-aware initialization as a minimal intervention to test the optimization-versus-representation question appears unexamined (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: On scenes with planar reflective surfaces and held-out views, compare vanilla training, reflection-initialized vanilla training, and a reflection-specialized method, reporting reflective-region held-out quality and geometry of the recovered virtual images.
main_risk: Curved reflectors violate the planar virtual-image construction, limiting the claim's scope to near-planar cases.
community_default_belief: Standard splat representations fundamentally cannot handle mirror-like appearance and need explicit reflection modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A view-dependent radiance field can legitimately encode a virtual scene behind the reflector; classical image-based rendering exploited exactly this, suggesting the optimum exists and is merely unreachable from standard initialization.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 2 reflective scenes, initialized versus vanilla, reflective-region held-out PSNR delta.
kill_threshold: Kill if reflection-aware initialization recovers under 30% of the gap to the specialized method on near-planar reflectors.

one_line_idea: Stratified-random initialization plus aggressive pruning matches heuristic adaptive densification end-to-end, showing the celebrated densify-split-prune machinery is replaceable by capacity-then-selection.
problem: The splat training recipe's densification heuristics add hyperparameters, sequential dependencies, and reproducibility friction, and are assumed load-bearing.
core_hypothesis: An overcomplete start (random primitives stratified by a cheap depth or point prior) followed by opacity-based pruning explores at least as good a solution set as incremental densification, because selection from excess capacity is an easier optimization problem than incremental growth.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched final primitive counts and compute, overcomplete-then-prune training will match adaptive densification on held-out-view quality and surface accuracy across standard scenes, and will show lower variance across seeds.
why_important: A selection-based recipe is parallelizable, more reproducible, and amenable to theory, and would retire a folkloric component from a widely used system.
why_possibly_novel: Prune-only training regimes at matched budgets with seed-variance reporting appear not to be systematically compared against densification (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement stratified overcomplete initialization at 2-4x target count with periodic opacity pruning to budget; compare against the standard recipe on quality, geometry, seed variance, and wall-clock on standard scenes.
main_risk: Peak memory during the overcomplete phase may be prohibitive at large scene scale, weakening the practicality claim even if quality matches.
community_default_belief: Adaptive densify-and-split is essential to reach good splat solutions; starting dense and pruning is wasteful and inferior.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In overparameterized optimization generally, pruning from excess capacity is competitive with growth; nothing about the splat objective obviously reverses that pattern, and the belief rests on the original recipe's ablations rather than a fair matched-budget test.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 3 scenes, prune-only versus standard recipe at matched counts.
kill_threshold: Kill if prune-only lags by over 0.5 dB PSNR or over 10% relative chamfer at matched budgets on most scenes.

one_line_idea: Feed-forward splat predictors fail on camera-baseline distribution shift, not scene-content shift: their generalization boundary is a property of the training rig geometry, measurable by a baseline-sweep protocol.
problem: Generalizable splat networks are evaluated on held-out scenes drawn from capture setups similar to training, so it is unknown which axis of novelty (content versus camera geometry) actually breaks them.
core_hypothesis: These models internalize the training distribution of relative camera baselines and triangulation angles; quality degrades smoothly with content novelty but falls off a cliff outside the trained baseline range, because their matching and fusion layers are tuned to specific disparity statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled protocol rendering the same scenes under sweeping camera baselines will show reconstruction quality collapsing beyond the training baseline range by margins far exceeding content-shift effects at matched difficulty, consistently across public feed-forward models.
why_important: It tells practitioners that rig geometry compatibility, not scene domain, is the deployment constraint, and motivates baseline-conditioned or baseline-augmented training.
why_possibly_novel: Disentangling camera-geometry shift from content shift for feed-forward reconstruction via matched-scene baseline sweeps appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render matched scene sets across parameterized baseline ranges, evaluate public feed-forward splat models trained on known rigs, and compare quality-versus-baseline curves against quality under content swaps at fixed baseline.
main_risk: Public models' training rig statistics are partially undocumented, requiring inference of the training range from model behavior itself.
community_default_belief: Feed-forward 3D models generalize or fail based on scene content similarity to training data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correspondence layers operate on disparity distributions set by rig geometry; content merely modulates texture, so geometry shift attacks the mechanism while content shift attacks only the appearance prior.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one model, one scene set, five baseline conditions, quality-versus-baseline curve.
kill_threshold: Kill if out-of-range baseline degradation is within 1.5x of matched content-shift degradation, showing content dominates after all.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: camera baseline distribution at test time

one_line_idea: Floater artifacts in splat reconstructions are primarily fossilized exposure and white-balance inconsistency, not sparse-view ambiguity: photometric-nuisance-controlled captures will eliminate most floaters at unchanged view counts.
problem: Floaters are blamed on insufficient views and treated with geometric priors and heuristics, yet casual captures with auto-exposure produce them even at high view density.
core_hypothesis: Frame-to-frame photometric inconsistency creates view-specific residuals that the optimizer explains by placing low-opacity primitives in free space near the camera path; exposure variation, not view sparsity, is the dominant floater generator in typical captures.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched captures differing only in exposure lock will show large differences in free-space density artifacts at identical view counts, and floater volume will correlate with measured inter-frame photometric drift across scenes, while subsampling locked-exposure views degrades gracefully without floater blowup.
why_important: If the cause is photometric bookkeeping, the fix is exposure modeling or capture guidance, which is far cheaper than the geometric-prior arms race, and reconstruction robustness claims should control for it.
why_possibly_novel: Causal attribution of floaters to photometric drift via controlled capture pairs, with a quantitative free-space-density metric against GT geometry, appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture scene pairs with locked versus auto exposure at matched trajectories, train identically, and quantify free-space density artifacts against GT or proxy geometry, regressing artifact volume on measured photometric drift.
main_risk: Locked exposure changes image quality in dark regions, introducing a different artifact source that must be audited.
community_default_belief: Floaters are a view-sparsity ambiguity problem to be solved with geometric regularization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The optimizer only invents free-space density when views disagree; geometry supplies consistent evidence while auto-exposure supplies systematic disagreement, making photometrics the parsimonious culprit.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One capture session plus one GPU-day: 3 scene pairs locked versus auto exposure, floater-volume comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if exposure lock reduces floater volume by under 30% relative, indicating sparsity is the dominant cause.

one_line_idea: Splat compression methods pass interpolation benchmarks while selectively destroying view-extrapolation ability, so compression papers systematically overstate fidelity for any consumer that leaves the capture path.
problem: Compression and pruning for splat scenes report near-lossless quality using held-out frames from the capture trajectory, the easiest possible test distribution.
core_hypothesis: Primitives that appear redundant under capture-path rendering carry disproportionate information for off-path views (parallax revelation of occluded structure), so compression tuned on interpolation deletes exactly the primitives extrapolation needs.
falsifiable_prediction: Across public compression methods, quality loss measured on off-path extrapolated cameras will exceed on-path loss by a large multiple at equal compression ratios, and the gap will widen with compression aggressiveness.
why_important: Compressed splat scenes are headed into maps, streaming, and embodied applications that render from arbitrary viewpoints; an interpolation-only validation culture ships silent quality regressions.
why_possibly_novel: Extrapolation-stratified evaluation of splat compression appears unpublished; the failure mode is predictable but unmeasured (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compress standard scenes at several ratios with public methods, render on-path held-out and synthesized off-path cameras against a GT-dense capture, and report the on-path versus off-path quality-loss ratio.
main_risk: Defining fair off-path GT requires dense hemispherical captures, limiting scene variety.
community_default_belief: Splat compression at reported ratios is visually lossless for practical purposes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Redundancy is defined relative to a view distribution; the methods measure redundancy on the capture path and the deployment distribution is broader, a textbook train-test mismatch hiding in the evaluation design.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one dense-capture scene, two compression methods, on-path versus off-path loss at two ratios.
kill_threshold: Kill if off-path quality loss is under 1.5x on-path loss at aggressive compression, showing extrapolation robustness.

one_line_idea: Dynamic splat representations interpolate time but cannot extrapolate it even fractions of a second, revealing they store appearance trajectories rather than motion models, measurable by a future-rendering cliff test.
problem: Time-conditioned splat representations are described as capturing scene dynamics, suggesting some motion understanding, but they are only ever evaluated at timestamps inside the training window.
core_hypothesis: These representations fit time-indexed appearance curves with no inductive bias toward physical motion continuation, so rendering quality collapses immediately outside the training time range, in contrast to even trivial constant-velocity geometric extrapolation.
falsifiable_prediction: Rendering at timestamps just beyond the training window will show quality falling off a cliff within a small fraction of a second, while a baseline that extrapolates per-primitive trajectories with constant velocity degrades far more gracefully on the same scenes.
why_important: World-model and robotics uses of 4D scene representations need short-horizon prediction; knowing that current representations have zero extrapolation defines the gap between scene capture and scene understanding.
why_possibly_novel: A time-extrapolation stress test for dynamic scene representations, with motion-model baselines as reference, appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train public dynamic splat methods on standard dynamic scenes truncated in time, render beyond the truncation against withheld real frames, and compare against constant-velocity and constant-acceleration primitive-trajectory extrapolators.
main_risk: Withheld-frame comparison confounds camera and scene motion; cameras must be held out at matched difficulty inside and outside the window.
community_default_belief: Time-conditioned 4D representations capture scene dynamics in a meaningful sense.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Their objective only rewards fitting observed timestamps; dynamics in the predictive sense is never supervised, so the capability has no reason to emerge, and the word dynamics oversells curve fitting.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one dynamic scene, truncated training, quality-versus-extrapolation-horizon curve with a constant-velocity baseline.
kill_threshold: Kill if trained representations match or beat constant-velocity extrapolation at 0.2 seconds beyond the window, showing genuine motion structure.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: rendering timestamp relative to training window

one_line_idea: Popping artifacts in splat rendering are localized depth-ordering errors fixable by exact small-k per-tile sorting only where a cheap ambiguity test triggers, giving artifact-free video at a bounded few-percent cost.
problem: Approximate global sorting in splat rasterization causes temporal popping under camera motion, and current mitigations either cost too much or only reduce frequency.
core_hypothesis: Ordering errors that produce visible popping are spatially sparse and predictable from local depth-overlap statistics, so exact ordering applied selectively to flagged tiles eliminates perceptible popping at a small constant overhead, rather than requiring globally correct ordering.
falsifiable_prediction: An ambiguity-gated exact-sort renderer will reduce temporal instability metrics on camera sweeps to the level of full exact sorting while adding only a bounded percentage to frame time, and flagged-tile prevalence will be small on standard scenes.
why_important: Temporal artifacts gate professional adoption of splat rendering for film previz and AR; a bounded-cost exactness result converts an approximation-quality argument into an engineering guarantee.
why_possibly_novel: Selective exactness driven by a measurable ambiguity predicate, with a temporal-stability evaluation protocol, appears unexplored for splat rasterization (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the gated sorter in an open rasterizer, define a flicker metric on rendered camera sweeps (temporal gradient energy at fixed pixels against a full-sort reference), and measure artifact reduction versus overhead across scenes.
main_risk: Ambiguity prediction may miss rare orderings that dominate perception, requiring conservative thresholds that inflate cost.
community_default_belief: Popping is an acceptable approximation artifact whose exact fix is too expensive for real-time rendering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The expensive part is sorting everything; perceptible errors come from a sparse subset identifiable in advance, and sparse exactness is cheap, a pattern proven in other rendering approximations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: gated sorter prototype, flicker metric on 3 scenes versus cost.
kill_threshold: Kill if removing perceptible popping requires exact sorting on over 20% of tiles or over 15% frame-time overhead.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: selective exact sorting gated by ambiguity test

one_line_idea: Implicit neural fields still beat explicit splats decisively on thin structures and view extrapolation, and a structure-stratified benchmark will show the representations are complements, not a settled succession.
problem: The community has largely declared explicit splatting the successor to implicit fields based on average benchmark quality and speed, without stratifying by scene structure type.
core_hypothesis: Continuous implicit representations retain advantages precisely where primitive-based discretization is mismatched: sub-primitive thin geometry, smooth extrapolation beyond capture views, and topology-free surfaces; aggregate benchmarks under-weight these regimes.
falsifiable_prediction: A stratified protocol (thin-structure chamfer, off-path view quality, watertightness) will show implicit methods winning those strata by clear margins while losing aggregate PSNR and speed, across matched scenes and budgets.
why_important: Representation choice is being made by aggregate leaderboards; a regime map prevents premature abandonment of the representation class that wins the regimes downstream applications care about.
why_possibly_novel: Structure-stratified head-to-head comparison at matched budgets, designed around regime discovery rather than a winner verdict, appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select scenes rich in thin structures with GT geometry, train representative implicit and explicit methods at matched compute, and report stratified geometry and view-quality metrics including off-path cameras.
main_risk: Matched-budget definitions favor one side depending on the axis (time versus memory versus quality); multiple budget definitions must be reported.
community_default_belief: Explicit splatting has superseded implicit fields for practical novel-view synthesis and reconstruction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The succession narrative is driven by speed and average-case quality on capture-path evaluations; discretization theory predicts specific structural regimes where continuous fields dominate, and those regimes are invisible in the averages.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: 3 thin-structure scenes, one method per family, stratified metric table.
kill_threshold: Kill if implicit methods fail to win thin-structure chamfer by at least 20% relative or off-path quality by at least 1 dB at matched budgets.

one_line_idea: Feed-forward pointmap reconstructors carry strong absolute scene-scale priors and will misreconstruct scale-anomalous scenes (miniatures, sets, macro shots) in a predictable direction, revealing memorized scale rather than inferred geometry.
problem: Pointmap-regression reconstruction models produce metric-looking outputs that are widely trusted, but their behavior on scenes whose true scale contradicts semantic priors has not been characterized.
core_hypothesis: These models resolve scale primarily from semantic content statistics (rooms are room-sized), so on scale-anomalous scenes they will confidently output prior-consistent scale rather than geometry-consistent scale, and the error will follow the semantic prior direction.
falsifiable_prediction: On miniature dioramas and macro captures with known GT dimensions, reconstruction scale error will be large, systematically biased toward canonical scale, and strongly reduced when semantic cues are removed (texture-swapped or geometry-only renders of the same shapes).
why_important: Metric trust in feed-forward reconstruction is spreading into robotics and measurement applications; knowing that scale is semantically inferred defines where the outputs can and cannot be trusted.
why_possibly_novel: Scale-anomaly probes with semantic-cue ablation for pointmap models appear unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble scale-anomalous captures with GT dimensions plus semantic-cue-ablated controls, run public feed-forward reconstructors, and report signed scale error distributions per condition.
main_risk: Miniature scenes also differ in depth-of-field statistics, which must be controlled or modeled to isolate the semantic pathway.
community_default_belief: Feed-forward reconstruction models infer geometry from multi-view and pictorial evidence, with priors as a soft regularizer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale is unobservable from geometry alone in most training pairs, so the loss forces models to learn semantic scale lookup as the primary mechanism, making prior-dominance the expected behavior, not the exception.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: 20 miniature and macro captures, signed scale-error histogram versus canonical-scale prediction.
kill_threshold: Kill if median absolute scale error on scale-anomalous scenes is under 15%, showing genuine geometric scale inference.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: scene scale anomaly and semantic-cue ablation

one_line_idea: Pose-free reconstruction models contain an implicit camera-intrinsics estimator whose bias is set by the training field-of-view distribution, and their pose errors on out-of-distribution lenses are predictable from that bias alone.
problem: Models that jointly infer geometry and cameras from raw images are treated as having solved calibration implicitly, with pose accuracy reported as aggregate statistics.
core_hypothesis: The implicit intrinsics estimate regresses toward the modal training field of view; on wider or narrower lenses, rotation and translation errors grow with a signature predictable from the intrinsics bias (focal-baseline compensation), rather than randomly.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating pose error across a lens sweep on matched scenes will show a systematic error component that a one-parameter focal-bias model explains most of, and supplying true intrinsics as a hint will remove that component while leaving residual error unchanged.
why_important: It converts unpredictable pose failure into a computable envelope per lens, tells users when a cheap intrinsics hint fixes things, and locates the next training investment (FOV diversity, intrinsics conditioning).
why_possibly_novel: Attribution of pose-free model errors to implicit-intrinsics bias via lens sweeps and hint interventions appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render or capture matched scenes across focal lengths, evaluate pose-free reconstructors with and without intrinsics hints, and decompose pose error into focal-bias-explained and residual components.
main_risk: Focal effects couple with composition changes at capture time; rendered sweeps avoid this but add domain gap.
community_default_belief: Pose-free reconstruction generalizes across cameras because geometry is inferred from correspondences, not from lens assumptions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correspondence fixes geometry only up to the projective ambiguity that intrinsics resolve; the network must guess intrinsics from content, and guesses inherit training-set bias by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: rendered focal sweep, one model, error-versus-focal curve with and without hints.
kill_threshold: Kill if the focal-bias component explains under 30% of out-of-distribution pose error variance, or hints fail to reduce error.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: lens field of view and intrinsics hinting

one_line_idea: Multi-task 3D foundation models suffer measurable gradient conflict between depth and pose heads specifically on dynamic-scene batches, and conflict-gated task weighting recovers accuracy on both without new data.
problem: Unified reconstruction models train depth, pose, and matching heads jointly on mixed static and dynamic data, assuming the tasks are mutually reinforcing.
core_hypothesis: On dynamic content the tasks disagree: pose heads need dynamic regions ignored while depth heads need them explained, producing systematic gradient conflict that damages both heads relative to conflict-managed training, with conflict magnitude spiking on dynamic batches.
falsifiable_prediction: Instrumenting per-head gradient cosine similarity during training will show conflict concentrated on dynamic-content batches, and interventions (conflict-gated weighting or dynamic-region gradient exclusion for pose) will improve both pose and depth metrics over the joint baseline at matched compute.
why_important: The field is consolidating on unified 3D models; understanding when their task mixture is self-defeating turns architecture folklore into a measurable training-dynamics fix.
why_possibly_novel: Batch-content-conditioned gradient-conflict analysis for 3D multi-task models, tied to a targeted intervention, appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrain a mid-scale unified reconstructor with gradient instrumentation on a mixed static/dynamic corpus, quantify conflict-versus-content statistics, then train the gated variant and compare pose and depth outcomes.
main_risk: Gradient cosine is a noisy conflict proxy; conclusions need corroboration via task-arithmetic or head-freezing controls.
community_default_belief: Joint training of geometry tasks is synergistic, with shared features benefiting all heads.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The static-world assumption that makes the tasks compatible is violated by dynamic content, and violation shows up exactly as inter-task gradient disagreement, which standard training silently averages away.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: instrumented fine-tuning run, conflict-versus-batch-content curve.
kill_threshold: Kill if dynamic-batch gradient conflict is within 20% of static-batch conflict, or if gating buys under 3% relative on both heads.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: batch content type and task-weighting policy

one_line_idea: Neural surface reconstruction can reach near-GT-supervised accuracy using only photometric and multi-view consistency, and a controlled supervision-ablation study will locate exactly which scenes still need 3D ground truth.
problem: High-accuracy surface reconstruction pipelines still assume 3D supervision (scans, depth sensors) somewhere in training, constraining data scale and domain coverage.
core_hypothesis: For most scene types, the information in dense multi-view photometric consistency saturates what 3D supervision provides; the genuinely GT-dependent residual is confined to identifiable regimes (low texture, strong view-dependence), so self-supervised surface learning can match supervised accuracy outside those regimes.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched models trained with photometric-only versus scan-supervised objectives will show near-equal chamfer and completeness on well-textured matte scenes, with the supervised advantage concentrating measurably in low-texture and high-glossiness strata.
why_important: If self-supervision suffices outside known regimes, surface-reconstruction training escapes the scanned-data bottleneck and can scale on ordinary video, with sensors reserved for the mapped hard regimes.
why_possibly_novel: A regime-resolved supervision-value map for surface learning, rather than aggregate benchmark deltas, appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched surface models under the two supervision regimes on scenes stratified by texture and material statistics, and report the supervised-minus-self-supervised accuracy gap per stratum.
main_risk: Photometric self-supervision is sensitive to calibration and exposure quality, which could masquerade as a fundamental gap.
community_default_belief: Serious surface accuracy requires 3D ground truth in training; photometric self-supervision is a weaker substitute across the board.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense multi-view constraints over-determine surfaces under Lambertian-adjacent conditions, and the belief may generalize from early methods whose failures were optimization artifacts since resolved.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: 4 scenes spanning texture strata, both objectives, per-stratum chamfer gap.
kill_threshold: Kill if the supervised advantage exceeds 15% relative chamfer even on well-textured matte strata.

one_line_idea: Scaling feed-forward 3D reconstruction is data-limited, not parameter-limited: multi-view scene data has low effective diversity per token, and a compute-matched scaling study will show exponents far below those driving 2D and language scaling optimism.
problem: The field extrapolates language-model scaling intuitions to 3D reconstruction transformers, but posed multi-view data is heavily redundant (thousands of near-identical frames per scene) and scene diversity, not frame count, may bound learning.
core_hypothesis: Reconstruction loss scales primarily with unique-scene count rather than total frames or parameters; frame-level scaling saturates quickly, making the effective scaling exponent with respect to compute much smaller than naive token counting suggests.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled grid over parameters, unique scenes, and frames-per-scene will show held-out reconstruction error nearly flat in frames-per-scene beyond a small number, strongly dependent on unique scenes, and parameter scaling saturating early at fixed scene diversity.
why_important: Roadmaps and budgets for 3D foundation models currently assume 2D-style returns to scale; measured exponents would redirect investment toward scene-diversity acquisition rather than model size.
why_possibly_novel: Public scaling analyses specific to multi-view reconstruction with scene-versus-frame decomposition appear absent (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a family of small-to-mid reconstructors on controlled subsets of a large scene corpus varying unique scenes and frames per scene at matched compute, and fit scaling curves per axis.
main_risk: Small-scale exponents may not transfer to frontier scale; the study bounds but does not settle frontier behavior.
community_default_belief: 3D reconstruction transformers will improve predictably with more data and parameters, mirroring 2D and language scaling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scaling laws assume approximately i.i.d. token novelty; multi-view frames violate this egregiously, and no measurement currently supports transplanting the exponents.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Three GPU-days: 3x3 grid over scenes and frames-per-scene at one model size, scaling-curve fit.
kill_threshold: Kill if frames-per-scene scaling remains strong (loss improvement above 10% per doubling) out to 64 frames per scene, contradicting the redundancy hypothesis.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: unique-scene count vs frames-per-scene vs parameters

one_line_idea: Recurrent-memory reconstruction models have an effective spatial memory horizon of only a few keyframes: a loop-revisitation probe will show geometry consistency decaying with intervening content, exposing sequential state as the bottleneck for long-form 3D perception.
problem: Streaming 3D models with recurrent state are described as maintaining persistent scene memory, but no protocol measures how much geometry that state actually retains over long trajectories.
core_hypothesis: The recurrent state compresses recent observations well but overwrites older scene geometry roughly monotonically with new content volume, so revisited areas are re-reconstructed inconsistently unless revisitation is recent, with a measurable half-life in keyframes.
falsifiable_prediction: On trajectories that leave and re-enter mapped areas with controlled intervening content, cross-visit geometry consistency (relative pose of re-reconstructed structure, depth agreement) will decay smoothly with intervening keyframe count, yielding a half-life far below trajectory lengths typical of real deployments.
why_important: Persistent-memory claims underpin using these models for embodied mapping; a measured half-life defines when external memory or map fusion is mandatory and gives architects a concrete target metric.
why_possibly_novel: A revisitation-consistency protocol with parametric intervening-content control for recurrent 3D models appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct or select trajectories with controlled loop closures, run public streaming reconstructors, and measure cross-visit depth and structure agreement as a function of intervening keyframes.
main_risk: Disentangling memory decay from viewpoint-difference effects at revisit requires matched revisit geometry across conditions.
community_default_belief: Recurrent scene-state models maintain a persistent map of what they have seen within a session.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fixed-size state under streaming updates is a lossy compressor; without an explicit retention objective, gradient descent favors recency, and nothing in current training rewards long-horizon retention.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: synthetic loop trajectories at 3 intervening-content levels, one model, consistency-versus-gap curve.
kill_threshold: Kill if cross-visit consistency shows no significant decay out to 200 intervening keyframes, demonstrating true persistence.

one_line_idea: Full cross-view attention in reconstruction transformers is mostly spent rediscovering epipolar geometry: constraining attention to epipolar neighborhoods after a coarse pose estimate retains accuracy at large compute savings.
problem: Multi-view reconstruction transformers attend all-to-all across view tokens, making compute quadratic in views and blocking high-view-count scenes, on the assumption that unconstrained attention learns something geometry cannot provide.
core_hypothesis: After coarse pose estimation, the useful attention mass concentrates near epipolar-consistent token pairs; hard-restricting attention to dilated epipolar bands preserves nearly all reconstruction accuracy because off-band attention encodes redundant global context obtainable more cheaply.
falsifiable_prediction: Measured attention distributions of trained models will concentrate near epipolar bands, and retrofitted band-restricted attention will retain reconstruction accuracy within a small margin at severalfold attention-compute reduction, scaling to view counts the dense model cannot process.
why_important: It makes many-view feed-forward reconstruction tractable, and settles whether unconstrained attention learns geometry beyond epipolar structure or merely re-derives it expensively.
why_possibly_novel: Epipolar-restricted attention exists in stereo contexts; a concentration measurement on trained general reconstructors plus a retrofit-parity claim at scale appears new (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Quantify attention mass versus epipolar distance in a public reconstructor, retrofit banded attention with fine-tuning, and compare accuracy and compute across view counts against the dense baseline.
main_risk: Coarse pose errors corrupt the bands exactly on hard scenes, potentially removing the mechanism when it is most needed; band dilation must be error-adaptive.
community_default_belief: Unconstrained cross-view attention is worth its cost because it learns correspondences and context jointly beyond what geometric constraints capture.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Epipolar geometry is a hard constraint on where correspondence evidence can be; attention outside it can only carry context whose information content is low-rank and cheaply summarized.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: attention-versus-epipolar-distance histogram on one trained model; if off-band mass is high and irreducible, the retrofit claim dies early.
kill_threshold: Kill if banded attention loses over 5% relative reconstruction accuracy at 4x attention savings after fine-tuning.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: attention support restriction to epipolar bands

one_line_idea: Single-image 3D generators are dominated by canonical-shape retrieval: counterfactual probes that decouple texture identity from geometric evidence will show outputs following the recognized category, not the visible geometry.
problem: Image-to-3D models produce plausible shapes that are interpreted as geometric inference from the image, but plausibility is equally consistent with memorized category templates.
core_hypothesis: When visible geometric evidence (contours, shading, self-occlusion) contradicts the canonical shape of the recognized category, these models follow the category prior; genuine geometric evidence-following is limited to small deformations around templates.
falsifiable_prediction: On counterfactual renders (category-typical texture applied to atypical geometry and vice versa), reconstruction chamfer to true geometry will be systematically worse than chamfer to the category-canonical shape, demonstrating retrieval dominance, with the effect shrinking only for categories with high training shape diversity.
why_important: Applications from AR asset capture to robotic interaction assume the output reflects the actual object; retrieval dominance means silent shape errors precisely on unusual instances, and the probe quantifies the boundary.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic texture-geometry counterfactual evaluation of image-to-3D models with a retrieval-versus-evidence decomposition appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct counterfactual asset pairs by swapping textures across geometries within and across categories, render single views, run public image-to-3D models, and compare output-to-truth versus output-to-canonical chamfer.
main_risk: Defining category-canonical shapes requires care; using training-set nearest neighbors as the canonical reference is more defensible but heavier.
community_default_belief: Modern image-to-3D models reconstruct visible geometry and hallucinate only the unseen parts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Single-view geometry is deeply ambiguous and the training objective rewards distributional plausibility; retrieval of typical shapes minimizes expected loss, so retrieval is what optimization should produce.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 30 counterfactual pairs, one model, truth-versus-canonical chamfer comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if outputs track true geometry over canonical shape (truth chamfer lower in over 70% of counterfactual cases).

one_line_idea: Rolling-shutter skew and motion blur are exploitable metric side channels: they encode absolute velocity and hence absolute scale, recoverable by a learned estimator to metrically calibrate monocular reconstruction without IMU or intrinsics.
problem: Monocular reconstruction is scale-ambiguous in the idealized projective model, so systems bolt on IMUs, known objects, or learned semantic priors for metric scale.
core_hypothesis: Real cameras break the ambiguity: rolling-shutter row-time skew and exposure-time blur length are absolute-time-stamped measurements of image motion, and jointly with estimated relative geometry they determine metric scale; a learned extractor of these micro-cues can calibrate scale within useful bounds on ordinary video.
falsifiable_prediction: On video with GT trajectories, a shutter-artifact-based scale estimator will recover absolute scale with bounded relative error on sequences with sufficient motion, degrade predictably as shutter speed increases, and beat semantic-prior scale baselines on scenes lacking familiar objects.
why_important: A physics-based scale channel that needs no extra hardware would upgrade every monocular pipeline to metric output and decouple scale from semantic familiarity.
why_possibly_novel: Rolling-shutter and blur are treated as nuisances to remove; their deliberate use as a metric scale oracle in learned reconstruction appears unexplored (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the estimator on video with known camera timing and GT motion, evaluate scale recovery versus GT trajectories across motion regimes and shutter settings, and ablate against semantic-scale baselines.
main_risk: Modern sensors with fast readout and short exposures shrink the signal toward noise floor; the operating envelope may be narrow.
community_default_belief: Monocular metric scale must come from external sensors or semantic priors, because the projective ambiguity is fundamental.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The ambiguity theorem assumes a global-shutter pinhole with instantaneous exposure; real image formation is time-resolved, and time plus motion gives metric leverage the idealization hides.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: controlled captures at varied shutter settings with GT motion, scale-recovery error versus signal-strength curve.
kill_threshold: Kill if median scale error exceeds 25% on sequences with strong motion and slow shutter, where the signal should be strongest.

one_line_idea: Elaborate positional encodings in point cloud transformers are mostly redundant with kNN graph topology: an encoding-ablation study will show local connectivity carries the signal, collapsing a crowded design axis.
problem: Point transformer variants compete on increasingly complex relative positional encodings, with gains attributed to better geometric awareness.
core_hypothesis: Once local neighborhoods are defined by kNN graph construction, most geometric information is already in the connectivity and edge vectors; sophisticated positional encodings mainly re-encode this, so radically simplified encodings will match performance across 3D tasks that do not require fine metric detail.
falsifiable_prediction: Sweeping encoding complexity at fixed graph construction on 3D object detection and registration will show near-flat task metrics, while corrupting graph construction at fixed encoding degrades sharply, establishing where the information actually enters.
why_important: It would redirect architecture research from encoding design to neighborhood construction, and simplify production models without accuracy loss.
why_possibly_novel: Factorized attribution between graph construction and positional encoding appears missing from point-architecture ablation culture (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched point transformers with encodings from none through state-of-the-art at fixed kNN policy, plus graph-corruption controls, on standard 3D detection (box mAP) and registration (recall) benchmarks.
main_risk: Tasks demanding fine metric discrimination (surface normal estimation) may genuinely need rich encodings, restricting the claim's scope.
community_default_belief: Relative positional encoding design is a primary driver of point transformer performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reviewer culture rewards encoding novelty, so ablations rarely test the null that connectivity suffices; message passing over kNN edges already computes relative geometry implicitly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: two encoding tiers on one detection benchmark at fixed graph policy.
kill_threshold: Kill if removing rich encodings costs over 2 points of box mAP or over 5% registration recall at fixed graph construction.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: positional encoding complexity vs graph construction

one_line_idea: Object-centric 3D pretraining transfers poorly to scene-level tasks because it learns closed-surface completion priors that actively mislead on open scene geometry, a measurable negative-transfer effect.
problem: 3D representation learning still leans on object datasets for pretraining, assuming object-level geometric knowledge transfers upward to scenes.
core_hypothesis: Object pretraining instills watertight-shape completion biases; scene data is open, partial, and clutter-dominated, so the prior misleads reconstruction and detection near occlusion boundaries, producing negative transfer that grows with pretraining strength on object data.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched fine-tuning runs from object-pretrained, scene-pretrained, and random initializations will show object-pretrained models underperforming scene-pretrained and, near occlusion boundaries specifically, sometimes underperforming random initialization, with error concentrated in hallucinated-closure patterns.
why_important: It challenges a default pretraining recipe and identifies which geometric priors are portable across the object-scene divide, informing corpus design for 3D foundation models.
why_possibly_novel: Negative-transfer attribution via boundary-stratified error and closure-pattern analysis appears missing from 3D pretraining studies (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched backbones on object versus scene corpora, fine-tune on scene reconstruction and 3D detection, and evaluate boundary-stratified geometric error plus a closure-hallucination statistic.
main_risk: Corpus size and quality confound with corpus type; matched-budget curation is essential and hard.
community_default_belief: Any large 3D pretraining corpus helps scene tasks; object data is a convenient and effective source.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Priors are not generically transferable; a completion prior is anti-correlated with truth on open geometry, and aggregate metrics have been hiding the boundary-localized damage.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: two initializations, one scene task, boundary-stratified error comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if object-pretrained initialization matches scene-pretrained within 5% relative on boundary-stratified metrics, showing no meaningful negative transfer.

one_line_idea: Masked point-cloud pretraining learns sensor sampling patterns more than geometry: cross-sensor transfer tests will show performance collapse that tracks sampling-density mismatch rather than shape content.
problem: Masked autoencoding on point clouds is credited with learning geometric structure, but pretraining and evaluation usually share a sensor family with fixed sampling statistics.
core_hypothesis: The reconstruction pretext is solvable largely by modeling scan-pattern regularities (ring structure, density falloff, dropout patterns); representations therefore encode sensor signatures, and transfer across sensor types will degrade in proportion to sampling-statistics distance, even at identical scene geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: Evaluating pretrained encoders on the same scenes resampled under different sensor simulations will show downstream 3D detection and registration drops that correlate with a sampling-statistics divergence measure, while geometry-preserving density normalization recovers much of the loss.
why_important: 3D foundation models are expected to serve heterogeneous fleets of sensors; sensor-signature learning would explain brittle transfer and prescribe density-invariant pretext designs.
why_possibly_novel: Controlled same-geometry cross-sensor resampling as a probe of what point pretraining learned appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate multiple sensor sampling patterns over identical scene geometry, pretrain on one pattern, evaluate downstream tasks across patterns with and without density normalization, and regress performance drop on sampling divergence.
main_risk: Sensor simulation fidelity limits external validity; a real two-sensor rig subset is the confirmatory anchor.
community_default_belief: Masked point modeling learns transferable geometric representations of shapes and scenes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The pretext loss is dominated by predicting where points are, and point placement is mostly a sensor property; geometry is the residual, not the main signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one pretrained encoder, two simulated sensors on identical scenes, downstream delta versus divergence.
kill_threshold: Kill if cross-sensor degradation is under 10% relative after density normalization, showing geometry dominates the representation.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: sensor sampling pattern at fixed geometry

one_line_idea: Built-in rotation invariance in point cloud architectures destroys pose information that registration and manipulation actually need, and augmentation-trained equivariant-by-learning models dominate on a pose-sensitivity-stratified task suite.
problem: Rotation-invariant architectures are promoted as principled solutions for point cloud learning, evaluated mostly on classification-style tasks where invariance is harmless.
core_hypothesis: Hard-wired invariance discards orientation information irreversibly; on pose-sensitive tasks (registration, grasp-relevant orientation estimation) invariant architectures underperform augmentation-trained standard architectures, and the deficit tracks how much task output depends on absolute or relative orientation.
falsifiable_prediction: A task suite ordered by pose sensitivity will show invariant architectures matching on pose-free tasks and falling progressively behind on pose-sensitive ones, with registration recall gaps opening at tight rotation-error thresholds.
why_important: It replaces an ideology (invariance is principled) with a decision rule (match architecture invariance to task pose sensitivity), preventing systematic architecture mismatches in robotics stacks.
why_possibly_novel: A pose-sensitivity-stratified comparison isolating the invariance design axis at matched capacity appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched invariant and standard architectures with equal augmentation budgets on a task ladder from shape classification through registration at multiple error thresholds, and plot performance gap versus task pose sensitivity.
main_risk: Capacity matching across architecture families is imperfect; multiple size points per family are needed.
community_default_belief: Building rotation invariance into the architecture is strictly preferable to learning it from augmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Invariance is information destruction; tasks that need the destroyed information cannot recover it, while augmentation-trained models can modulate invariance per task demand.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one invariant and one standard model on registration at three rotation-error thresholds.
kill_threshold: Kill if invariant architectures stay within 5% relative registration recall at the tightest threshold, showing no pose-information deficit.

one_line_idea: Lifting frozen 2D foundation features onto 3D points already saturates much of what 3D self-supervised learning achieves, so 3D SSL should be measured by its margin over the 2D-lifting baseline, which is rarely reported.
problem: 3D self-supervised methods report gains over training-from-scratch baselines, while the practically available alternative (project 2D foundation features onto points via known calibration) is usually absent from comparison tables.
core_hypothesis: For RGB-paired 3D data, most representational value in current 3D SSL is semantic and already present in 2D features; the genuine 3D-specific margin (fine geometry, occlusion structure) is small and task-dependent, and honest baselines would reframe the subfield's progress narrative.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 3D detection and registration tasks on RGB-paired benchmarks, a tuned 2D-feature-lifting baseline will land within a small margin of leading 3D SSL pretraining on most metrics, with 3D SSL retaining clear advantages only on geometry-pure tasks or RGB-absent regimes.
why_important: Compute allocated to 3D pretraining should buy something 2D models cannot provide; measuring the true 3D-specific margin redirects the field toward that residual.
why_possibly_novel: A standardized lifting baseline with careful fusion tuning as a mandatory comparator appears absent from 3D SSL evaluation culture (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a strong lifting baseline (multi-scale 2D features, visibility-aware projection, light fusion head), evaluate against public 3D SSL checkpoints across tasks, and report per-task margins.
main_risk: Lifting quality depends on calibration and visibility handling; a weak lifting implementation would overstate the 3D SSL margin.
community_default_belief: 3D self-supervision learns representations qualitatively beyond what 2D models projected to 3D can offer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: 2D models saw orders of magnitude more data; most 3D benchmark signal is recognizable from appearance, and geometry-specific residuals are smaller than subfield rhetoric implies.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: lifting baseline versus one 3D SSL checkpoint on one detection benchmark.
kill_threshold: Kill if 3D SSL beats the tuned lifting baseline by over 10% relative on most RGB-paired tasks, confirming a substantial 3D-specific margin.

one_line_idea: Learned registration features fail in the low-overlap regime for a specific reason, local ambiguity without global layout reasoning, and overlap-stratified evaluation plus a layout-hypothesis stage will both prove and fix it.
problem: Point cloud registration reports high average recall, but real scanning workflows fail exactly on low-overlap pairs, suggesting the averages hide a regime problem.
core_hypothesis: Feature-based registration is fundamentally local: below an overlap threshold, correct correspondences exist but are statistically indistinguishable from ambiguous matches without scene-layout priors, so recall collapses sharply rather than degrading gracefully, and only global layout reasoning (room-shape priors, symmetry hypotheses) can push the frontier lower.
falsifiable_prediction: Overlap-stratified evaluation will show a sharp recall cliff below roughly 15-20% overlap for leading methods, correspondence quality analysis will show correct matches present but unranked, and a layout-hypothesis re-ranking stage will recover a meaningful fraction of failures without touching the features.
why_important: Low-overlap capability determines scanning cost (fewer captures) and robot exploration efficiency; knowing the failure is ranking, not detection, redirects method design.
why_possibly_novel: The correct-but-unranked diagnosis and layout-hypothesis re-ranking for low-overlap registration appear unexamined (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify standard registration benchmarks by exact overlap, analyze rank positions of geometrically correct correspondences in the ambiguity regime, and evaluate the re-ranking stage's recall recovery.
main_risk: Layout priors may not generalize beyond indoor rectilinear scenes, bounding the fix's scope.
community_default_belief: Registration failure at low overlap reflects missing correspondence information that better local features will eventually supply.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information bottleneck is disambiguation, not detection; locally identical structures repeat in built environments, and no local feature can rank between them by construction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: overlap-stratified recall plus correct-match rank analysis on one benchmark.
kill_threshold: Kill if correct correspondences are absent (not merely unranked) in over half of low-overlap failures, refuting the ranking diagnosis.

one_line_idea: Point cloud upsampling networks hallucinate plausible-looking surface detail that measurably corrupts downstream pose estimation and registration, making upsampling a negative-value preprocessing step for geometric pipelines.
problem: Learned upsampling is marketed as enhancing sparse scans for downstream use, validated by visual quality and point-to-surface metrics on the upsampling task itself.
core_hypothesis: Upsamplers interpolate with shape priors that are wrong in the tails; the hallucinated points carry confident but biased geometry that downstream estimators weight as evidence, degrading registration and pose accuracy relative to running directly on the sparse input.
falsifiable_prediction: Registration and object-pose pipelines fed upsampled clouds will show worse rotation and translation errors than the same pipelines on raw sparse clouds, with degradation concentrated where the upsampler's prior mismatches true geometry (edges, thin parts, unusual shapes).
why_important: A pipeline stage that improves its own metric while harming consumers is a systems trap; quantifying it changes how enhancement modules must be evaluated (always downstream).
why_possibly_novel: Downstream-task audits of point upsampling appear rare to absent; the subfield evaluates on intrinsic metrics (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched registration and pose benchmarks on raw versus upsampled inputs across sparsity levels and upsampling methods, stratifying error by local geometry type.
main_risk: Some downstream estimators may benefit at extreme sparsity where any densification helps; the claim needs sparsity-regime boundaries.
community_default_belief: Densifying sparse point clouds with learned upsamplers is a safe or beneficial preprocessing step for downstream geometry tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Downstream estimators assume measurement noise models; hallucinated points violate those models with spatially correlated bias, which is worse than honest sparsity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one upsampler, one registration benchmark, raw-versus-upsampled error comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if upsampled inputs match or beat raw inputs on registration error across sparsity levels, showing no downstream tax.

one_line_idea: Discarding range-image structure by converting scans to unordered points throws away the sensor noise model, and architectures that retain scan-grid structure will beat point-set models on odometry at matched capacity.
problem: The default abstraction for scan processing is the unordered point set, which discards acquisition structure (scan order, per-ring noise, angular sampling) that carries information about measurement reliability.
core_hypothesis: Sensor noise is structured in the acquisition grid (range-dependent per-beam noise, incidence-angle effects); models operating on range images can learn implicit per-measurement reliability weighting that point-set models cannot recover after unordering, yielding better odometry and mapping accuracy especially in high-noise regimes.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched-capacity range-image and point-set odometry models trained on identical data will show the range-image models achieving lower trajectory error, with the gap widening on high-noise and long-range strata and shrinking when point-set inputs are augmented with explicit per-point noise features.
why_important: It identifies the representation choice as a noise-modeling decision rather than a convenience, and the noise-feature-recovery experiment quantifies exactly what information the point abstraction loses.
why_possibly_novel: Framing range-image superiority as implicit noise-model learning, with a feature-recovery falsification, appears untested (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched odometry models on range-image versus point-set representations of identical scans, evaluate trajectory error stratified by noise regime, then add explicit noise features to the point-set model and measure gap closure.
main_risk: Range-image models may win through unrelated inductive biases (2D convolution efficiency); the noise-feature-recovery arm is essential for attribution.
community_default_belief: Unordered point sets are the canonical, information-sufficient representation for scan geometry.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Points are measurements, not geometry; stripping acquisition metadata is lossy for exactly the reliability information that estimation theory says optimal fusion needs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: both representations on one odometry benchmark, noise-stratified trajectory error.
kill_threshold: Kill if range-image models fail to beat point-set models by at least 10% relative trajectory error in high-noise strata, or if noise features close under 30% of the gap (attribution fails).

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: representation (range image vs point set) and noise-feature recovery

one_line_idea: Content-adaptive keyframe selection, not longer context, is the binding constraint in long-video understanding: a learned selector at 10% frame budget can retain nearly all of full-context accuracy across video reasoning tasks.
problem: Long-video models compete on context length, paying quadratic or streaming costs to ingest frames most of which are redundant for any given query.
core_hypothesis: Information relevant to video-level understanding is concentrated in a small, identifiable subset of frames; a query-conditioned selector trained to maximize downstream answer quality can find it, making frame budget a soft constraint and context-length competition mostly wasteful.
falsifiable_prediction: On long-video question answering and temporal reasoning benchmarks, the selector at a 10% frame budget will retain at least 95% of full-context accuracy of the same backbone, and will beat uniform and shot-boundary sampling at matched budgets by clear margins.
