why_important: A validated selection-beats-context result changes the economics of video understanding at deployment scale and refocuses research on relevance inference rather than context engineering.
why_possibly_novel: Query-conditioned selection trained end-to-end against answer quality, evaluated as a context-compression frontier across budgets, appears underexplored relative to context-extension work (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a lightweight selector over frozen frame embeddings with answer-quality reward on public long-video benchmarks, and map the accuracy-versus-budget frontier against uniform, shot-based, and full-context baselines.
main_risk: Tasks requiring dense temporal integration (counting, continuous state tracking) may resist sparse selection, bounding the claim to retrieval-style understanding.
community_default_belief: Long-video understanding progress requires architectures that ingest ever more frames.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human viewers answer most video questions from a handful of glances; the redundancy structure of video makes dense ingestion an artifact of architecture convenience rather than task necessity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: frozen backbone, simple relevance selector, accuracy-versus-budget curve on one benchmark.
kill_threshold: Kill if the selector at 10% budget retains under 90% of full-context accuracy on the majority of tested tasks.

one_line_idea: For revisitation-heavy long videos, a geometric 3D scene buffer beats learned appearance-token memories of the SAM2 style at re-localizing content after long absences, because place is a stronger long-horizon key than appearance.
problem: Streaming video memory architectures store recency-weighted appearance tokens, which decay or drift over long horizons; revisitation after minutes is a known weak point.
core_hypothesis: Registering observations into a persistent metric 3D buffer (via online reconstruction and camera tracking) provides a memory keyed by place rather than appearance recency; for content re-identification after long absences in the same environment, place-keyed lookup will beat appearance-token memory at matched compute, with the advantage growing with absence duration.
falsifiable_prediction: On long egocentric and walkthrough videos with revisitation ground truth, the geometric-buffer system will exceed appearance-memory baselines, including a SAM2-memory-style contrast baseline repurposed for point re-localization, on post-absence re-identification position accuracy, with the gap increasing monotonically in absence duration.
why_important: It tests whether the future of video memory is learned token banks or explicit spatial world models, a fork with large architectural consequences for embodied and assistant applications.
why_possibly_novel: Direct capability comparison of geometric versus learned memory under controlled absence-duration sweeps appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument long revisitation-rich videos with GT correspondence across visits, implement the geometric buffer from public reconstruction components, and compare against learned-memory trackers on re-identification versus absence duration and compute.
main_risk: Reconstruction drift in long sequences corrupts the buffer's keys; loop-closure quality becomes the hidden variable.
community_default_belief: Scaling learned memory banks is the path to long-horizon video understanding, with geometry as an optional extra.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Appearance changes with lighting and viewpoint while place coordinates do not; a memory keyed by the stable variable should win long horizons on first principles.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: 10 revisitation videos, geometric buffer versus one learned-memory baseline, re-identification accuracy at two absence durations.
kill_threshold: Kill if the geometric buffer fails to beat appearance memory by at least 10% relative re-identification accuracy at absences over 60 seconds.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: memory keying (geometric place vs appearance tokens)

one_line_idea: Video self-supervised representations pass action benchmarks largely on static appearance: dynamics-isolating probes (motion-only stimuli, frame-shuffle controls) will show most benchmark skill survives temporal destruction.
problem: Video SSL models are credited with learning motion and temporal structure, but the benchmarks used to certify them are known to be partially solvable from single frames.
core_hypothesis: The representational share attributable to genuine dynamics is small: probes evaluated under frame-shuffling, single-frame, and appearance-removed (motion-vector-only) conditions will reveal that current video SSL performance is dominated by static appearance, with true temporal structure contributing a minor share.
falsifiable_prediction: For leading video SSL checkpoints, downstream probe accuracy under frame-shuffled inputs will retain most of the intact-input accuracy on standard benchmarks, while on appearance-removed motion stimuli accuracy will collapse toward chance, jointly demonstrating appearance dominance.
why_important: World-model ambitions rest on video models understanding dynamics; a rigorous decomposition tells the field whether current pretraining objectives buy any of that, and which benchmarks can certify it.
why_possibly_novel: Single-frame solvability of benchmarks is known; a systematic three-way decomposition (intact, shuffled, appearance-removed) applied to modern video SSL checkpoints as a standard audit appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate public video SSL models under the three input conditions across action and temporal-reasoning benchmarks, and report the dynamics share (intact minus shuffled) per model and benchmark.
main_risk: Shuffling introduces distribution shift beyond temporal destruction; motion-preserving controls (reversed, speed-perturbed) refine attribution.
community_default_belief: Video self-supervision learns temporal dynamics beyond static appearance, which is why it beats image pretraining on video tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Video SSL objectives are optimized on data where appearance predicts labels well; gradient descent buys accuracy in the cheapest currency available, and that currency is appearance.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one checkpoint, intact-versus-shuffled probe accuracy on one benchmark.
kill_threshold: Kill if frame-shuffling costs over 40% relative accuracy on standard benchmarks, showing dynamics genuinely dominate.

one_line_idea: Long-video benchmarks are answerable from tiny frame subsets: an oracle frame-selection audit will show most questions need under 1% of frames, meaning the benchmarks measure retrieval, not long-form temporal understanding.
problem: Benchmarks advertising hour-scale video understanding drive architecture research toward long contexts, but no audit establishes how much of each benchmark actually requires long-range temporal integration.
core_hypothesis: For most benchmark questions, there exists a tiny frame subset sufficient for a frozen model to answer correctly; question types genuinely requiring cross-video integration (duration reasoning, repeated-event counting, narrative causality across acts) are a small minority, so long-context gains reported on these benchmarks mostly reflect better retrieval.
falsifiable_prediction: An oracle search over frame subsets will find that a large majority of questions are answerable at high accuracy from under 1% of frames, and per-question oracle-subset size will predict which architectures win, with long-context models excelling only on the large-subset minority.
why_important: The field is spending heavily on context extension justified by these benchmarks; an information-locality audit would redirect both benchmark design and architecture investment.
why_possibly_novel: Oracle-subset-size profiling as a benchmark-auditing methodology for long video appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: For each benchmark question, greedily search frame subsets with a frozen video-language model to find minimal sufficient sets, and report the distribution of minimal-set sizes and its correlation with model-family performance.
main_risk: Oracle search is expensive and its greedy approximation may overestimate minimal sizes; sampling questions mitigates cost.
community_default_belief: Strong performance on hour-scale video benchmarks certifies long-range temporal understanding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Question writers gravitate to localizable facts because they are easy to verify; the benchmark construction process itself selects for retrieval-style questions.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 200 sampled questions, greedy subset search with one frozen model, minimal-set-size histogram.
kill_threshold: Kill if under 50% of questions are answerable from under 1% of frames, showing the benchmarks do demand long-range integration.

one_line_idea: Video foundation models are near chance at judging the arrow of time on physics-driven footage, a capability gap invisible to every mainstream benchmark and decisive for world-model claims.
problem: Temporal directionality (irreversibility from friction, diffusion, gravity, causality) is a basic property of physical dynamics, yet no standard evaluation measures whether video models represent it.
core_hypothesis: Because pretraining objectives are nearly symmetric under time reversal and human-edited video contains reversed and looped content, current video representations encode little arrow-of-time signal; probes will be near chance on physics-driven clips while succeeding on clips with semantic directionality cues (people walking forward).
falsifiable_prediction: Linear probes on frozen video features for forward-versus-reversed classification will perform near chance on physics-dominated clips (falling, mixing, breaking) while performing well when semantic cues are present, and the physics-clip performance will not improve with model scale within current families.
why_important: The arrow of time is a minimal necessary condition for physical world modeling; certifying its absence gives a crisp, cheap target that pretraining objectives must fix before grander claims stand.
why_possibly_novel: Arrow-of-time probing exists as an older self-supervision task; using it as a stratified capability audit of modern foundation models with physics-versus-semantics decomposition appears new (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble physics-dominated and semantics-dominated clip sets, train forward/reverse probes on frozen features of public video models across scales, and report stratified accuracy and scale trends.
main_risk: Compression artifacts can leak direction; artifact-free renders or re-encoded controls are required.
community_default_belief: Large video models implicitly learn physical dynamics including temporal directionality from massive pretraining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in the objective distinguishes forward from backward for most content; capabilities do not emerge without an optimization reason, however large the data.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: 500 physics clips forward and reversed, one frozen model, probe accuracy.
kill_threshold: Kill if physics-clip arrow-of-time probe accuracy exceeds 70% for current models, showing the capability exists after all.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: temporal direction and content stratum (physics vs semantic)

one_line_idea: Event-order understanding in video-language models rides on editing artifacts: on continuous single-shot footage their before/after accuracy will collapse, revealing shot grammar, not temporal reasoning, as the learned mechanism.
problem: Video-language models score well on temporal-order questions, and this is cited as evidence of temporal reasoning, but most training and benchmark footage is edited, where cuts and shot conventions encode order.
core_hypothesis: Models learned to read editing grammar (shot changes, framing conventions, montage patterns) as an order signal; on unedited continuous footage where order must be inferred from state changes in the world, before/after accuracy will drop toward chance while edited-footage accuracy stays high.
falsifiable_prediction: A matched question set posed on edited versus continuous single-shot versions of comparable events will show a large accuracy gap, and ablating cut boundaries (smoothing transitions) on edited footage will degrade accuracy despite identical event content.
why_important: Temporal reasoning is a headline claim for video-language systems entering robotics and monitoring; knowing the mechanism is editorial parsing changes both trust boundaries and training-data strategy.
why_possibly_novel: Edited-versus-continuous controlled comparison with cut-ablation interventions for temporal-order evaluation appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate event-matched edited and single-shot clip pairs, pose identical order questions to public models, and run cut-ablation interventions on the edited set.
main_risk: Event matching across footage styles is imperfect; synthetic staging of identical events in both styles strengthens the control at added cost.
community_default_belief: Order-question accuracy demonstrates that video-language models track temporal structure of events.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Editing conventions are a far easier and more consistent signal than physical state inference, and models exploit the easiest sufficient signal by default.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 100 matched pairs, one model, edited-versus-continuous accuracy gap.
kill_threshold: Kill if single-shot accuracy is within 10 points of edited-footage accuracy, showing genuine state-based order inference.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: editing structure presence (edited vs single-shot, cut ablation)

one_line_idea: Storing motion state (tracked positions, velocities, and a sparse dynamics summary) instead of appearance tokens halves video-memory cost at equal long-horizon tracking accuracy, because appearance is re-observable but motion history is not.
problem: Streaming video architectures allocate memory to appearance embeddings of past frames, in the style popularized by SAM2 memory banks, and memory size becomes the scaling bottleneck for long sessions.
core_hypothesis: Appearance information is largely recoverable from the current frame plus a compact identity code, while motion history (velocities, trajectories through occlusion) is unrecoverable once discarded; a memory that prioritizes kinematic state over appearance snapshots achieves equal or better long-horizon tracking and re-identification at a fraction of the storage.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched memory budgets on long tracking evaluations, kinematic-state memory will match appearance-token memory at full budget and dominate it at reduced budgets, with the crossover advantage growing as budget shrinks, measured by long-horizon position accuracy and post-occlusion recovery.
why_important: Memory economics decide what runs on-device and how long sessions can be; identifying which information is actually irreplaceable gives a principled compression target rather than heuristic token eviction.
why_possibly_novel: An information-recoverability framing for video memory design, with controlled budget-matched comparisons of kinematic versus appearance storage, appears unexplored (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement both memory types over a shared frozen backbone, evaluate long-video point and object tracking at multiple memory budgets, and map accuracy-versus-budget curves for each memory design.
main_risk: Strong appearance changes at reappearance (lighting, deformation) may require more appearance memory than the hypothesis allows; identity codes must be tested under appearance drift.
community_default_belief: Richer appearance memories are the primary driver of robust long-horizon video tracking.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The world re-supplies appearance every frame; what the past uniquely provides is dynamics, and current designs hoard the recoverable quantity while discarding the unrecoverable one.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: both memories at two budgets on one long-tracking benchmark, accuracy-versus-budget comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if kinematic memory needs over 70% of appearance-memory budget to match its accuracy, showing no meaningful compression advantage.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: memory content type (kinematic state vs appearance tokens)

one_line_idea: Video models encode absolute frame rate as a hidden covariate: speed-perception probes will reveal systematic bias when test frame rate differs from the training distribution, corrupting all downstream motion judgments.
problem: Video models are deployed across content with heterogeneous frame rates under the assumption that temporal normalization layers or sampling handle the difference.
core_hypothesis: Models internalize the modal training frame rate as an implicit clock; motion-speed judgments, action-duration estimates, and dynamics predictions all inherit a multiplicative bias equal to the train-test frame-rate ratio, rather than being frame-rate invariant.
falsifiable_prediction: Probes estimating object speed or event duration from frozen features will show errors that scale linearly with the train-test frame-rate ratio, and the bias will persist under naive resampling but disappear when frame timestamps are provided to models designed to consume them.
why_important: Motion-sensitive applications (sports analysis, driving, manufacturing) mix camera types freely; a hidden clock assumption produces systematic misjudgments that are cheap to fix once measured.
why_possibly_novel: Frame-rate bias curves for foundation video models, measured via speed and duration probes across resampled content, appear unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Resample videos with known GT motion at several frame rates, evaluate speed and duration probes on frozen features per rate, and fit the bias-versus-ratio relationship across model families.
main_risk: Resampling artifacts (judder, blur differences) confound pure rate effects; high-frame-rate source material downsampled cleanly is required.
community_default_belief: Standard temporal sampling makes video models effectively frame-rate agnostic.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nothing in the architecture receives absolute time; the only clock available during training is the frame index, so the model must calibrate motion in frame units, which breaks the moment the frame-time mapping changes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one model, three frame rates on GT-motion clips, speed-probe bias curve.
kill_threshold: Kill if speed-probe bias is under 10% across a 2x frame-rate change, demonstrating effective rate invariance.

one_line_idea: Repetitive-action counting is already latent in frozen video features as periodic token-trajectory structure, extractable by spectral analysis without any counting-specific training.
problem: Action counting is treated as a specialized task requiring dedicated architectures and annotation, and general video models are not credited with the capability.
core_hypothesis: Repetitive motion imprints periodic structure on the trajectory of frame and patch tokens through feature space; frequency-domain analysis of these trajectories recovers repetition frequency and count without supervision, and count accuracy from frozen features will approach trained counting systems.
falsifiable_prediction: A training-free spectral estimator over frozen features of public video models will achieve counting accuracy within a modest margin of supervised counting baselines on standard repetition benchmarks, with failures concentrated where the repetition is subtle relative to camera motion.
why_important: It demonstrates that capability extraction can substitute for task-specific training, gives practitioners a zero-training counting tool, and provides a clean probe of what temporal structure pretraining actually encodes.
why_possibly_novel: Spectral readout of token trajectories as a training-free counting method with a quantified gap to supervised systems appears unexplored (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement trajectory extraction and robust period estimation over frozen features, evaluate on public repetition-counting benchmarks against supervised references, and ablate across backbone families and layers.
main_risk: Camera motion injects competing periodicities; stabilization or motion-compensated tokens may be needed, which weakens the training-free story.
community_default_belief: Counting repetitions requires task-specific supervision or architectures with explicit period modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Any representation that tracks appearance over time must oscillate with the content; the information is necessarily present, and the only question is the noise floor of the readout.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: spectral estimator on one benchmark subset with one backbone, count-error comparison to published supervised numbers under matched protocol.
kill_threshold: Kill if training-free count error exceeds 2x the supervised reference error on the standard benchmark.

one_line_idea: The egocentric-video performance gap is mostly a camera-motion-statistics gap, not a content gap: motion-matched resampling of exocentric data will close much of it without collecting new egocentric footage.
problem: Egocentric benchmarks lag despite huge exocentric pretraining corpora, and the standard response is collecting more first-person data, an expensive and privacy-sensitive path.
core_hypothesis: The transfer gap is dominated by unfamiliar camera-motion statistics (head-driven rotation, motion parallax patterns) rather than by unfamiliar content; augmenting or resampling exocentric data to match egocentric motion statistics recovers a large share of the gap at zero collection cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Models pretrained on motion-matched exocentric data will close a substantial fraction of the egocentric transfer gap on anticipation and temporal-localization tasks, while content-matched but motion-unmatched controls close little of it, isolating motion statistics as the causal factor.
why_important: It converts an expensive data-collection problem into a cheap augmentation problem, and identifies which invariances video pretraining fails to acquire.
why_possibly_novel: Causal decomposition of the egocentric gap into motion versus content components via matched resampling appears untested (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate camera-motion statistics from egocentric corpora, build motion-matched exocentric pretraining sets via crop-trajectory augmentation, pretrain matched models, and evaluate egocentric transfer against unmatched and content-matched controls.
main_risk: Synthetic crop trajectories approximate but do not replicate real head motion parallax, which requires depth-aware augmentation to simulate properly.
community_default_belief: Egocentric understanding requires egocentric-specific pretraining data because first-person content is fundamentally different.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The content of egocentric video (kitchens, hands, objects) is abundantly present in exocentric corpora; what is genuinely rare is the camera behavior, and no one has isolated the two factors.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: fine-tune with motion-matched versus standard exocentric augmentation, egocentric task delta.
kill_threshold: Kill if motion-matched pretraining closes under 20% of the egocentric transfer gap while content controls close a similar amount.

one_line_idea: Video models covertly exploit codec structure: evaluated on artifact-free renders or re-encoded footage, motion-sensitive task performance will shift measurably, revealing compression as an unacknowledged input feature.
problem: Nearly all video training data is compressed, and compression encodes motion explicitly in its block and artifact structure, yet evaluations never control for codec effects.
core_hypothesis: Models learned to read compression side channels (blocking patterns, artifact gradients that correlate with motion vectors); performance on motion-sensitive tasks will drop on pristine uncompressed or differently-encoded footage, and artifact-only inputs (residual visualizations) will carry surprising task signal.
falsifiable_prediction: Matched evaluation across codec conditions (original, re-encoded at different settings, artifact-free renders) will show systematic performance shifts on motion-sensitive tasks exceeding those on static-appearance tasks, and probes trained on artifact-only inputs will beat chance substantially on motion tasks.
why_important: Codec dependence is a hidden domain-shift axis that breaks deployments on professional or synthetic footage, and it contaminates scientific conclusions about what models learned from pixels.
why_possibly_novel: Codec-stratified capability evaluation with artifact-only probes appears absent from video model evaluation practice (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct codec-condition variants of benchmark subsets with GT labels preserved, evaluate public models per condition on motion-sensitive and static tasks, and train artifact-only probes as a signal-existence check.
main_risk: Re-encoding changes low-level statistics beyond motion channels; multiple codec families and quality tiers are needed to isolate the motion-specific pathway.
community_default_belief: Compression artifacts are nuisance noise that large-scale training teaches models to ignore.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Artifacts are informative, not noise: they are a deterministic function of motion and texture, and models exploit any informative channel; ignoring free information would be the anomaly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one model, one motion-sensitive task, original versus artifact-free condition delta.
kill_threshold: Kill if codec-condition performance shifts are under 3% relative on motion-sensitive tasks and artifact-only probes are at chance.

one_line_idea: Pixel-space next-frame prediction spends its capacity on texture advection, not dynamics: a loss-decomposition study will show physics-relevant errors are a vanishing share of the training signal, explaining why video predictors fail physics probes despite low loss.
problem: Next-frame prediction is treated as a road to physical world models, but models with excellent prediction loss still fail simple physical-plausibility probes, and the disconnect is unexplained.
core_hypothesis: The pixel loss is dominated by texture transport terms (most pixels move predictably with local flow), while dynamics-decisive pixels (contact events, direction changes, occlusion births) contribute negligibly to the gradient; consequently optimization converges to advection engines with no pressure to model dynamics, and the loss-share imbalance quantitatively predicts the physics-probe failure.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing prediction loss into advection-explainable and dynamics-critical components across training will show the dynamics share to be tiny and shrinking as loss falls, and reweighting training toward dynamics-critical pixels will improve physics probes at slight cost in overall loss.
why_important: It explains a central disappointment of the generative-video program mechanistically and provides an actionable fix (event-weighted objectives) with a measurable target.
why_possibly_novel: Gradient-share decomposition between advection and dynamics components of video prediction loss appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the decomposition using flow-based advection baselines to define residual dynamics pixels, instrument training of a mid-scale predictor, and run the reweighting intervention with physics-probe evaluation.
main_risk: Defining dynamics-critical pixels via flow residuals partially bakes in the conclusion; independent event annotations on a subset guard against circularity.
community_default_belief: Scaling next-frame prediction will progressively force models to learn physical dynamics because prediction ultimately requires it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Prediction requires dynamics only for the pixels where dynamics bites, and those pixels are so rare that the optimizer can ignore them essentially forever at current scales.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: loss decomposition on a pretrained predictor over benchmark clips, dynamics-share measurement.
kill_threshold: Kill if the dynamics-critical share of the loss gradient exceeds 15%, or if reweighting fails to move physics probes by at least 10% relative.

one_line_idea: Object permanence in video trackers and memory models fails past a measurable occlusion-duration threshold, and the failure is architectural (memory decay) rather than perceptual, testable by a duration-sweep protocol with location prediction through occlusion.
problem: Trackers and memory-based video models, including SAM2-style memory-bank designs used as contrast baselines here, claim robustness to occlusion, but evaluations rarely parameterize occlusion duration, so nobody knows where permanence actually breaks.
core_hypothesis: Permanence-like behavior in current systems is short-horizon memory persistence, not object-state inference: predicted-location accuracy through occlusion decays smoothly with duration and collapses beyond a threshold set by memory capacity and decay dynamics, while systems with explicit dynamics state (even simple constant-velocity models) degrade far more slowly.
falsifiable_prediction: A controlled occlusion-duration sweep on procedurally occluded footage will show learned-memory systems collapsing to near-chance localization beyond a few seconds, with the collapse point shifting with memory size, while an explicit kinematic-state baseline holds usable accuracy several times longer.
why_important: Permanence horizons determine reliability for surveillance, robotics, and assistive systems; a measured horizon with architectural attribution tells builders whether to buy memory or dynamics.
why_possibly_novel: Duration-parameterized permanence testing with memory-size ablation and kinematic baselines appears unpublished as a systematic protocol (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate matched sequences with parameterized full-occlusion durations, evaluate reappearance-time localization accuracy across memory-based systems at multiple memory sizes and kinematic baselines, and map collapse thresholds.
main_risk: Procedural occlusion may miss real-world reentry appearance changes; a real annotated subset anchors the synthetic findings.
community_default_belief: Modern memory-based video architectures durably represent occluded objects and re-acquire them on reappearance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Memory banks store observations, not world state; without a dynamics model the best possible readout is the last observation, whose relevance decays with everything that moves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: duration sweep at 4 durations, one memory system versus constant-velocity baseline.
kill_threshold: Kill if the learned-memory system maintains localization within 2x of its short-occlusion error out to 10-second occlusions, showing durable permanence.

family_fingerprint.subject_system: occlusion handling in memory-based video systems

one_line_idea: Lifting multi-object tracking into reconstructed 3D turns heavy occlusion from a failure regime into a solvable geometry problem: 3D-buffer tracking will dominate 2D association precisely in the occlusion-density stratum where benchmarks are hardest.
problem: Multi-object tracking still operates predominantly in image space, where occlusion destroys evidence and identity switches concentrate, and gains from better 2D association have plateaued in crowded scenes.
core_hypothesis: Most occlusion in crowded scenes is a projection artifact: objects remain separated in 3D even when overlapped in 2D; tracking in a metrically reconstructed frame (via monocular or multi-view geometry) removes the ambiguity at its source, so identity preservation improves specifically as 2D occlusion density rises, rather than uniformly.
falsifiable_prediction: On driving and pedestrian benchmarks with 3D ground truth, a geometry-lifted tracker will show identity-preservation and trajectory-accuracy gains over matched 2D-association baselines that grow monotonically with per-scene occlusion density, with negligible gains in sparse scenes.
why_important: It relocates the tracking bottleneck from association heuristics to reconstruction quality, giving the field a clear capability path (better geometry, better tracking) with quantified regime boundaries.
why_possibly_novel: Occlusion-density-stratified attribution of 3D lifting benefits, isolating where geometry pays, appears missing from tracking literature (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a lifted tracker from public reconstruction and detection components, evaluate against 2D baselines on 3D-annotated benchmarks with per-scene occlusion-density scoring, and report stratified identity and trajectory metrics.
main_risk: Monocular reconstruction errors in cluttered scenes may inject more noise than occlusion removes, inverting the benefit exactly where it is needed.
community_default_belief: Tracking progress comes from better appearance embeddings and association logic in image space; 3D lifting is an expensive niche for instrumented platforms.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information destroyed by projection cannot be recovered by association cleverness, while feed-forward reconstruction has quietly become cheap and accurate enough to run per frame.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: lifted versus 2D tracker on one 3D-annotated benchmark, occlusion-density-stratified identity metrics.
kill_threshold: Kill if the lifted tracker's advantage in the top occlusion-density quartile is under 10% relative on identity-preservation metrics.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: tracking coordinate frame (2D image vs reconstructed 3D)

one_line_idea: Feed-forward dynamic-scene reconstruction can match per-scene-optimized 4D methods on geometry metrics within a bounded gap while being orders faster, making optimization-based 4D a transitional technology, and the gap map tells us where optimization still pays.
problem: Dynamic-scene reconstruction is dominated by per-scene optimization taking minutes to hours, blocking interactive and robotics applications, while feed-forward alternatives are assumed to be far behind in quality.
core_hypothesis: For the geometry that downstream consumers use (depth, 3D trajectories, camera poses), feed-forward dynamic reconstructors already sit within a modest, quantifiable gap of optimization methods on most scene types, with the true optimization advantage confined to identifiable regimes (long sequences, extreme deformation, fine view-dependent detail).
falsifiable_prediction: A matched-protocol comparison on dynamic benchmarks with GT geometry will show feed-forward methods within a bounded relative gap on depth and 3D-trajectory accuracy for a majority of scene strata, at orders-of-magnitude lower latency, with the residual gap concentrated in predictable strata.
why_important: If the gap is small where it matters, real-time dynamic 3D perception is already practical, and per-scene optimization should be repositioned as a refinement stage rather than the default.
why_possibly_novel: A stratified geometry-first gap analysis between reconstruction paradigms, rather than rendering-quality comparisons, appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate public feed-forward and optimization-based 4D methods under one protocol on dynamic datasets with GT depth and trajectories, stratify by motion magnitude, sequence length, and texture, and report gap maps with latency.
main_risk: Protocol choices (alignment conventions, scale normalization) can swing comparisons; the protocol must be preregistered and symmetric.
community_default_belief: Per-scene optimization is necessary for trustworthy dynamic-scene geometry; feed-forward methods are fast previews.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The belief is anchored on rendering-quality comparisons where optimization shines; geometry metrics may tell a different story because feed-forward models amortize strong data priors that optimization must rediscover per scene.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one feed-forward and one optimization method on one dynamic benchmark, depth and trajectory gap with latency.
kill_threshold: Kill if the feed-forward geometry gap exceeds 30% relative on most strata, confirming optimization necessity.

one_line_idea: Piecewise-rigid motion priors generalize to fast, unfamiliar dynamics better than learned free-form deformation fields, and a motion-magnitude-stratified 3D tracking comparison will show the crossover point where learned flexibility becomes a liability.
problem: Dynamic reconstruction methods increasingly rely on unconstrained learned deformation fields, which fit training-like motion beautifully but have no guarantees on out-of-distribution dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Physical scenes are dominated by piecewise-rigid motion; free-form deformation fields buy accuracy on soft deformation at the cost of catastrophic failure on fast rigid motion outside training statistics, while piecewise-rigid parameterizations degrade gracefully everywhere, creating a measurable regime crossover.
falsifiable_prediction: On dynamic scenes stratified by motion speed and rigidity, learned deformation fields will win on slow non-rigid strata but lose to piecewise-rigid parameterizations on fast strata by growing margins, with 3D trajectory error as the deciding metric.
why_important: Deformation parameterization is a core design choice in every 4D system; a regime map replaces aesthetics-driven choices with measured boundaries.
why_possibly_novel: Controlled rigidity-versus-speed stratification of deformation parameterizations under one protocol appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit matched 4D reconstructions with free-form versus piecewise-rigid motion models on stratified dynamic data with GT 3D trajectories, and report error by stratum with crossover identification.
main_risk: The piecewise-rigid decomposition into parts is itself estimated and its errors could be misattributed to the parameterization class.
community_default_belief: Flexible learned deformation fields are the most general and therefore best default for dynamic scene modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Generality without inductive bias means unbounded hypothesis spaces on unseen motion; rigidity is a physical prior that holds approximately almost everywhere and pays exactly when data runs out.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: two parameterizations on fast-motion scenes, 3D trajectory error comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if free-form fields stay within 15% relative trajectory error of piecewise-rigid models on the fastest motion stratum.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: motion model class vs motion regime

one_line_idea: Video-diffusion priors in dynamic reconstruction pipelines improve photorealism metrics while leaving geometric accuracy unchanged or worse, and a geometry-photometrics decomposed evaluation will expose the conflation driving their adoption.
problem: Generative video priors are being added to monocular dynamic reconstruction with claims of resolving ill-posedness, evaluated mostly by combined or perceptual metrics.
core_hypothesis: Diffusion priors hallucinate plausible appearance that satisfies perceptual metrics but supply no geometric constraint; decomposed evaluation will show gains concentrated in photometric and perceptual scores with flat or negative movement in depth, trajectory, and camera accuracy, revealing that the priors address the presentation, not the ill-posedness.
falsifiable_prediction: Across pipelines with and without generative priors at matched budgets, geometric metrics on GT-annotated dynamic scenes will differ by less than the photometric metrics by a large factor, and in occluded-region completion the prior-equipped methods will show confident but geometrically wrong structure at measurable rates.
why_important: Resource allocation and safety-relevant trust both depend on whether generative priors add geometric information or decoration; a decomposed protocol prevents category errors in method selection.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic geometry-versus-photometrics decomposition of generative-prior contributions in dynamic reconstruction appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run prior-equipped and prior-free dynamic reconstruction on GT-geometry benchmarks, report decomposed metric deltas, and audit occluded-region completions against GT for confident-wrong rates.
main_risk: Some prior-equipped pipelines entangle the prior with pose estimation, making clean ablation require reimplementation effort.
community_default_belief: Generative video priors meaningfully constrain the ill-posed parts of monocular dynamic reconstruction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A prior trained to produce plausible pixels enforces distributional realism, not instance-level geometric consistency; the two are orthogonal, and only the first is being measured by current protocols.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one pipeline pair on one benchmark, decomposed metric table.
kill_threshold: Kill if generative priors improve geometric metrics by over half their photometric improvement (relative terms), showing genuine geometric contribution.

one_line_idea: Discrete keyframe-based 4D representations with learned interpolators beat continuously time-conditioned fields on rapidly changing scenes, because continuous conditioning imposes an implicit temporal smoothness prior that fast dynamics violate.
problem: Continuous time conditioning is the default for neural 4D representations on the assumption that continuity in the parameterization is harmless or beneficial.
core_hypothesis: Networks conditioned on continuous time coordinates spectrally bias toward slow temporal variation, systematically underfitting rapid transitions (impacts, direction reversals); keyframed discrete states with learned interpolation allocate capacity at transitions and will win on motion-transient-heavy content at matched budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: On dynamic scenes stratified by temporal-change rate, continuous-time models will show error spikes localized at motion transients that keyframed models avoid, with the aggregate advantage flipping between strata and transient-localized error differing by large factors.
why_important: Temporal parameterization is a foundational choice for 4D scene capture; a measured spectral-bias account tells designers when each parameterization wins rather than following convention.
why_possibly_novel: Attribution of transient underfitting to temporal spectral bias, with keyframe crossover analysis, appears unexamined in the 4D literature (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched continuous and keyframed 4D models on transient-rich and smooth dynamic scenes, evaluate time-resolved geometry and rendering error around annotated transients, and test frequency-encoding interventions on the continuous model.
main_risk: Frequency-encoding tricks may rescue continuous models, converting the dichotomy into a tuning question, which the intervention arm addresses.
community_default_belief: Continuous time conditioning is the natural and adequate way to represent scene dynamics in neural fields.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Spectral bias of coordinate networks is well documented in space; its temporal consequences on transient-heavy real motion are unexamined convention, not validated design.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: both parameterizations on one impact-rich scene, transient-localized error comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if continuous-time models with standard frequency encodings match keyframed models within 10% relative on transient-localized error.

one_line_idea: Camera-object motion separation in monocular dynamic reconstruction degenerates predictably under near-forward camera motion, and quantifying the degeneracy prevalence in real corpora will show it affects a large share of driving and walking footage.
problem: Dynamic reconstruction methods assume camera and object motion are separable from image evidence, but epipolar-based separation is mathematically weak when object motion is near-parallel to camera translation.
core_hypothesis: For forward-translating cameras (driving, walking), objects moving along the camera axis produce image motion nearly indistinguishable from static geometry at wrong depth; methods silently resolve the ambiguity with priors, producing confident depth-speed errors whose prevalence in real footage is high and unmeasured.
falsifiable_prediction: A degeneracy score computed from GT geometry (angle between object motion and epipolar direction) will predict reconstruction error spikes across methods, and scoring real corpora will show a substantial fraction of dynamic content in the near-degenerate zone.
why_important: If a large share of practical footage sits near degeneracy, published average metrics dramatically understate risk for driving-adjacent applications, and method development should target the actual failure geometry.
why_possibly_novel: Prevalence measurement of motion-separation degeneracy in real corpora, linked to per-method error prediction, appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define the degeneracy score, validate error prediction on GT-annotated dynamic benchmarks across methods, then score large unlabeled corpora to estimate real-world prevalence.
main_risk: GT-annotated data sparse in the degenerate zone may limit validation power; synthetic augmentation of degenerate configurations fills the gap.
community_default_belief: Modern dynamic reconstruction robustly separates camera and object motion outside contrived corner cases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The corner case is geometrically generic for forward locomotion, which is the dominant camera motion of embodied platforms; rarity intuitions come from orbit-style capture datasets.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: degeneracy scoring plus error correlation on one annotated benchmark.
kill_threshold: Kill if degeneracy score explains under 20% of dynamic-region error variance, or if under 10% of real forward-motion footage falls in the near-degenerate zone.

one_line_idea: Transporting a fixed set of Gaussians along estimated scene flow, instead of re-densifying per timestep, reconstructs dynamic scenes with severalfold fewer primitives at equal quality, because dynamic scenes reuse geometry that current 4D methods keep re-creating.
problem: Dynamic splat methods manage primitives per timestep or with time-varying attributes, and their memory grows steeply with sequence length even when the scene contains the same objects throughout.
core_hypothesis: Physical persistence means the primitive set should be nearly constant with only poses changing; coupling a persistent primitive set to an explicit 3D motion field (transport instead of respawn) matches rendering and geometry quality at a fraction of primitive count and naturally yields 3D trajectories as a byproduct.
falsifiable_prediction: On standard dynamic scenes, transport-based models will match per-timestep-managed baselines within a small quality margin at 3-5x fewer primitives, and their emergent trajectories will track GT 3D motion where available, validating the persistence assumption.
why_important: Memory is the deployment bottleneck for 4D capture; persistence-based compression is principled (it encodes the physics) rather than heuristic, and the trajectory byproduct serves downstream perception.
why_possibly_novel: Persistent-set transport with explicit flow coupling, evaluated for compression ratio at matched quality and trajectory fidelity, appears not systematically established (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement transport-coupled dynamic splatting over public flow and reconstruction components, compare against per-timestep baselines at matched quality on primitive count, memory, and trajectory accuracy.
main_risk: Topology changes (objects entering, breaking, extreme deformation) violate persistence and need a measured exception mechanism whose frequency bounds the savings.
community_default_belief: Dynamic scenes require timestep-adaptive primitive management because content changes too much for a fixed set.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Almost all apparent change in real scenes is motion of persistent matter, not creation of new matter; the representation should mirror that, and current designs conflate motion with content change.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: transport prototype on 2 scenes, quality-versus-primitive-count comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if matching baseline quality requires over 60% of the baseline primitive count, showing negligible persistence savings.

one_line_idea: Temporal smoothing losses that make video depth look stable actively destroy true depth change, and an approach-sequence evaluation (time-to-contact fidelity) will show stabilized models are worse than their unstabilized versions for dynamic consumers.
problem: Video depth methods add temporal-consistency objectives tuned to eliminate flicker, evaluated by stability metrics that reward constancy regardless of whether the scene actually changed.
core_hypothesis: Consistency losses penalize genuine depth changes (approaching objects, camera push-in) as if they were noise, biasing models toward temporal inertia; on sequences with real depth dynamics, stabilized models will systematically lag true depth change, corrupting derived quantities like time-to-contact that safety consumers rely on.
falsifiable_prediction: On approach and push-in sequences with GT, stabilized models will show phase lag and magnitude attenuation in depth-change tracking relative to per-frame versions, with time-to-contact errors growing with the consistency-loss weight while flicker metrics improve monotonically.
why_important: The field is optimizing a proxy (stability) that anti-correlates with the safety-relevant signal (change fidelity) in exactly the scenarios that matter most; the tradeoff must be measured and reported.
why_possibly_novel: Change-fidelity evaluation (lag, attenuation, time-to-contact error) as a counterweight to stability metrics appears absent from video-depth evaluation practice (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or configure models across consistency-loss weights, evaluate on approach-rich GT sequences with lag, attenuation, and time-to-contact metrics alongside standard stability metrics, and publish the tradeoff frontier.
main_risk: Some consistency formulations may be change-aware (flow-compensated) and escape the critique; the study must stratify by formulation type.
community_default_belief: Temporal consistency is an unambiguous quality axis for video depth: more stable is better.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Stability metrics cannot distinguish suppressed noise from suppressed signal; optimizing them without a change-fidelity counterpart is unconstrained in the direction that harms dynamic use cases.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one stabilized and one per-frame model on approach sequences, lag and time-to-contact comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if stabilized models show under 5% time-to-contact error increase at strong stabilization, proving the tradeoff negligible.

family_fingerprint.subject_system: temporal consistency objectives for video depth

one_line_idea: Classical low-rank trajectory bases still beat learned motion representations for non-rigid structure recovery on low-texture deformable objects, defining a data-regime boundary the deep 4D literature ignores.
problem: Deep dynamic reconstruction has displaced classical non-rigid structure-from-motion machinery (low-rank trajectory and shape bases) without regime-resolved comparisons, especially on texture-poor deformables where learned matching is weakest.
core_hypothesis: Low-rank temporal structure is a strong, correct prior for many deformables (cloth, faces, organs); when texture is too poor for learned correspondence to shine, classical basis constraints extract more from the same observations, and a texture-by-method comparison will show a crossover the field assumes away.
falsifiable_prediction: On deformable sequences stratified by texture richness with GT 3D, learned methods will win high-texture strata while low-rank basis methods (possibly with learned features as input) win low-texture strata on 3D error, with hybrid variants dominating both.
why_important: Rehabilitating a discarded prior as a regime-specific winner both improves practical pipelines (hybridization) and corrects a monoculture drift in dynamic 3D research.
why_possibly_novel: Regime-resolved classical-versus-learned comparison on matched deformable data with hybrid arms appears missing from recent literature (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble texture-stratified deformable benchmarks with GT, run classical low-rank, learned, and hybrid methods under one protocol, and report stratified 3D error with crossover analysis.
main_risk: Classical methods need careful tuning to be fair; a weak classical implementation would fabricate the conclusion that deep methods dominate everywhere.
community_default_belief: Learned dynamic reconstruction has made classical non-rigid structure-from-motion priors obsolete.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The displacement happened on texture-rich benchmark content where learned correspondence excels; the priors encode temporal physics that data-driven methods must infer from correspondence they cannot get on texture-poor content.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: one classical and one learned method on low-texture deformable sequences, 3D error comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if learned methods match or beat low-rank baselines on low-texture strata by any margin, confirming obsolescence.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: texture richness stratum and method class

one_line_idea: Rolling-shutter row-time diversity within single frames can be exploited to super-resolve scene motion in time, recovering intra-frame 3D dynamics that global-shutter pipelines timestamp away.
problem: Fast intra-frame motion is invisible to standard video 3D pipelines that treat each frame as one time sample, and hardware solutions (high-speed or event cameras) are expensive and rare.
core_hypothesis: Rolling-shutter cameras sample each image row at a distinct known time, making every frame a temporal scan; modeling row time explicitly in dynamic reconstruction converts the shutter from an artifact source into a measurement channel, enabling temporal super-resolution of object trajectories well beyond the nominal frame rate.
falsifiable_prediction: On fast-motion scenes captured simultaneously with rolling-shutter and reference high-speed cameras, row-time-aware reconstruction will recover intra-frame trajectory structure (measured as trajectory error at sub-frame timestamps) far better than frame-time baselines, with accuracy tracking motion speed and shutter readout duration as theory predicts.
why_important: It extracts a high-speed-camera capability from commodity sensors by software alone, expanding who can study fast dynamics and improving dynamic reconstruction fidelity broadly.
why_possibly_novel: Rolling shutter is standard as a correction target; its deliberate use as a temporal super-resolution channel in learned dynamic reconstruction appears largely unexplored (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a dual-camera rig (rolling-shutter plus high-speed reference), capture controlled fast motions, extend a dynamic reconstruction model with row-time parameterization, and evaluate sub-frame trajectory recovery against the reference.
main_risk: Short readout times on modern sensors compress the intra-frame time span, and blur may dominate the row-time signal at extreme speeds.
community_default_belief: Rolling shutter is purely a distortion to be corrected; temporal resolution is set by frame rate and only hardware can raise it.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information-theoretic view says row-multiplexed timing is measurement, not noise; the correction convention discards a channel nobody priced.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One capture session plus one GPU-day: rotating-fan-style controlled target, row-time-aware versus frame-time reconstruction, sub-frame trajectory error.
kill_threshold: Kill if row-time-aware reconstruction improves sub-frame trajectory error by under 20% relative on fast-motion captures with long-readout sensors.

one_line_idea: Dynamic novel-view benchmarks are dominated by photometric quality variance rather than geometric fidelity: re-scoring published-style comparisons with geometry-only metrics will reorder methods and change which research directions look promising.
problem: 4D method comparisons rely on rendered-image quality metrics that mix geometric accuracy with appearance modeling and image priors, and the mixture ratio is unknown.
core_hypothesis: Method ranking variance on dynamic benchmarks is mostly attributable to appearance-modeling differences (color calibration, detail hallucination), so geometry-only re-evaluation (depth, trajectory, and camera accuracy) will produce substantially different orderings, revealing that the community optimizes appearance while believing it optimizes 4D structure.
falsifiable_prediction: For a set of public 4D methods, the rank correlation between image-quality orderings and geometry-only orderings on the same scenes will be low enough that at least a third of pairwise method comparisons flip, and the flips will concentrate among methods with generative or heavy appearance components.
why_important: Rank-driving metrics determine research investment; if geometry and photometrics disagree at this rate, the field's map of what works for 4D structure is unreliable and needs decomposed reporting.
why_possibly_novel: A systematic dual-ranking study across dynamic-scene methods with flip-rate quantification appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reproduce a slate of public 4D methods on GT-geometry dynamic benchmarks, compute both metric families under one protocol, and report rank correlations, flip cases, and their association with method architecture.
main_risk: Reproduction quality varies across public code; per-method verification against published behavior is needed before ranking claims.
community_default_belief: Rendered-image quality on held-out views is a faithful proxy for how well a method recovered dynamic scene structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Image metrics reward exactly the components (appearance priors, hallucinated detail) that are orthogonal to structure; the conflation is structural, not incidental.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two GPU-days: four methods on one benchmark, dual-metric rank comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if the two orderings agree with rank correlation above 0.85 and under 15% of pairwise comparisons flip.

one_line_idea: Defocus gradients across the frame are a single-image focal-length oracle: a probe exploiting depth-of-field structure will estimate intrinsics better than semantic-cue baselines, upgrading uncalibrated 3D pipelines for free.
problem: Single-image intrinsics estimation leans on semantic and vanishing-line cues, which fail in natural scenes without man-made structure, leaving uncalibrated reconstruction fragile exactly where it is most needed.
core_hypothesis: The spatial pattern of defocus blur across an image is jointly determined by aperture, focal length, and scene depth; combined with a monocular depth estimate, measurable defocus gradients over-constrain focal length, giving a physics-based estimator that works in structure-free natural scenes where geometric cues vanish.
falsifiable_prediction: On images with EXIF-verified intrinsics spanning apertures and scene types, the defocus-based estimator will beat vanishing-line and learned semantic baselines on focal-error percentiles in natural-scene strata, with accuracy degrading predictably as aperture narrows (signal vanishes at small apertures).
why_important: Reliable intrinsics from image content alone removes a gating input for metric monocular pipelines across archival, web, and consumer imagery.
why_possibly_novel: Depth-of-field structure as a primary intrinsics channel, fused with learned depth and validated against geometric-cue baselines per scene stratum, appears underexplored (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble EXIF-annotated image sets stratified by aperture and scene type, implement defocus-map extraction plus the joint solver, and compare focal-error distributions against baselines per stratum.
main_risk: Smartphone computational photography synthesizes or removes defocus, corrupting the physical signal on the most common image source.
community_default_belief: Single-image intrinsics estimation is fundamentally driven by geometric structure cues or brute-force learned priors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optics puts a second, independent channel in every photo; it is ignored because defocus is treated as an aesthetic property rather than a measurement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: 500 EXIF-verified images, defocus estimator versus one learned baseline, focal-error comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if the defocus estimator's median focal error is not at least 20% lower than baselines on wide-aperture natural-scene strata.

one_line_idea: Visual gravity-direction estimation from object and scene priors can reach IMU-competitive accuracy on typical footage, enabling orientation-aware vision on the billions of cameras without inertial data streams.
problem: Gravity direction is assumed to require an IMU, so vision pipelines either demand sensor fusion or operate gravity-blind, losing a powerful scene prior for reconstruction and understanding.
core_hypothesis: Scenes are saturated with gravity witnesses (standing people, hanging objects, liquid surfaces, architectural verticals, tree growth); a learned estimator aggregating these cues can recover gravity direction within about one degree for the large majority of frames on ordinary footage, sufficient for most downstream uses of IMU gravity.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets with IMU-derived GT orientation, the visual estimator will achieve a low-degree median error with a compact tail on typical handheld and vehicle footage, degrading predictably on witness-poor content (aerial ocean, close-ups), and its error will be uncorrelated with IMU drift regimes, making it complementary.
why_important: Gravity as a free pseudo-sensor improves reconstruction initialization, horizon stabilization, and physical reasoning wherever IMU data is absent, unsynchronized, or drifting.
why_possibly_novel: A dedicated gravity-estimation capability study with witness-taxonomy analysis and IMU-parity thresholds appears missing despite scattered use of vertical priors (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the estimator on orientation-annotated video, evaluate error CDFs per content stratum against IMU GT, and ablate cue families (people, architecture, liquids) to map witness contributions.
main_risk: Training-data orientation labels concentrate on upright cameras; extreme camera tilts may be underrepresented and fail exactly when stabilization is most needed.
community_default_belief: Reliable gravity estimation is an inertial-sensor capability; vision can offer only crude horizon heuristics.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Human observers judge vertical within a degree or two from images alone in most scenes, proving the visual information exists; no one has seriously engineered its extraction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: fine-tune a backbone for gravity regression on one orientation-annotated dataset, error CDF versus the one-degree target.
kill_threshold: Kill if median angular error exceeds 3 degrees on typical handheld footage, leaving no path to the one-degree regime.

one_line_idea: Out-of-distribution failure in learned camera pose regression is substantially a rotation-parameterization artifact: controlled parameterization swaps will show geodesic-aware outputs generalizing far better than the field's default choices at identical backbones.
problem: Pose regressors generalize poorly outside their training distribution, and the blame is placed on feature quality, while output parameterization (quaternions, Euler, 6D, procrustes-projected matrices) varies across papers without systematic OOD comparison.
core_hypothesis: Parameterizations differ in how regression errors map onto the rotation manifold; under distribution shift, extrapolation in the output space dominates failure, so manifold-respecting parameterizations degrade gracefully while chart-based ones fail at chart boundaries, producing large OOD differences invisible in-distribution.
falsifiable_prediction: Training identical backbones with different rotation parameterizations will show small in-distribution differences but large, systematic OOD differences on held-out viewpoint ranges, with error concentrated near parameterization singularities for chart-based outputs.
why_important: If a free design choice moves OOD robustness this much, every pose-adjacent system (relocalization, object pose, reconstruction initialization) can improve without new data or capacity, and papers must control for it before claiming feature-level conclusions.
why_possibly_novel: OOD-stratified, singularity-localized comparison of rotation parameterizations at matched backbones appears missing; existing comparisons are in-distribution (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched pose regressors under 4-5 parameterizations with controlled viewpoint-range splits, evaluate geodesic rotation error in and out of range, and localize errors relative to each parameterization's singular set.
main_risk: Interactions with loss choice (geodesic versus component losses) may dominate the parameterization effect; a loss-parameterization grid is required.
community_default_belief: Rotation parameterization is a minor implementation choice; generalization failures reflect feature and data limitations.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Regression extrapolates in output coordinates; coordinates with singularities and double covers make extrapolation pathological in ways training-range evaluation never exercises.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: two parameterizations, one OOD split, geodesic error gap.
kill_threshold: Kill if OOD geodesic error differs by under 10% relative across parameterizations at matched in-distribution error.

one_line_idea: Uncorrected radial distortion in training data leaves depth foundation models with a systematic depth-bowing fingerprint, detectable on flat surfaces and attributable to lens-distribution bias of the training corpora.
problem: Web-scale depth training mixes images from lenses with varied uncorrected distortion, and the geometric consequences on learned models are uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Models average over the training lens distribution, baking in a radially varying depth bias; predictions on verified-flat surfaces (walls, floors) will bow with image radius in a signature consistent across scenes, and the signature will differ between models trained on different corpus families, tracing it to data rather than architecture.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting planes to predicted depth on physically flat surfaces will reveal systematic radial residual profiles significantly different from zero, stable across scene content within a model, and differing across models with different training corpora.
why_important: A universal geometric bias corrupts all downstream metric uses (measurement, AR placement) in a correctable way; the fingerprint also provides corpus forensics for opaque training sets.
why_possibly_novel: Flat-surface radial-residual auditing as a lens-bias forensic for depth models appears unpublished (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect verified-flat-surface captures with calibrated cameras, run public depth models, fit planes, and analyze radial residual profiles per model with cross-scene stability tests.
main_risk: Perspective and shading gradients on flat surfaces could induce content-driven residuals mimicking lens bias; diverse orientations and materials control for this.
community_default_belief: Web-scale diversity averages out camera-specific artifacts, leaving depth models geometrically unbiased.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging over a biased lens population produces the population-mean distortion, not zero distortion; consumer optics share systematic radial characteristics rather than canceling.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: 30 flat-surface captures, two models, radial residual profiles.
kill_threshold: Kill if radial residuals are statistically indistinguishable from zero or unstable across scenes within each model.

one_line_idea: A camera-height prior over human-captured video (eye level and chest level dominate) yields metric scale within useful bounds for most consumer footage, formalizable as a drop-in probabilistic scale module for monocular pipelines.
problem: Monocular reconstructions of consumer video are scale-free, and existing metric fixes need intrinsics, sensors, or recognizable objects, all of which fail on large fractions of real footage.
core_hypothesis: The distribution of camera heights in human-captured video is tightly concentrated (handheld eye-level, chest-mounted, tripod bands); combining a ground-plane estimate with this prior determines scale probabilistically, and the posterior is accurate within 5-10% for the dominant capture modes, with identifiable failure flags for drone and mounted footage.
falsifiable_prediction: On video corpora with GT trajectories or scene scale, the height-prior module will deliver median scale error under 10% on handheld strata, calibrated posterior intervals with stated coverage, and reliable automatic flagging of out-of-prior capture modes via posterior dispersion.
why_important: Metric scale is the last missing ingredient for turning arbitrary consumer video into measurable 3D; a calibrated probabilistic module makes downstream consumers scale-aware with quantified uncertainty rather than false precision.
why_possibly_novel: Camera-height priors have been used informally in odometry; a calibrated, capture-mode-aware formulation with coverage guarantees and failure flagging appears missing (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate ground planes on GT-scaled sequences across capture modes, apply the prior-based solver, and report scale-error distributions, interval coverage, and flagging accuracy per stratum.
main_risk: Ground-plane estimation fails indoors with clutter and on non-flat terrain, coupling the module's reliability to a second estimator.
community_default_belief: Absolute scale for monocular video is unavailable without sensors, calibration, or known objects.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The capture process itself is a measurement device: humans hold cameras at biologically constrained heights, a prior as informative as many sensors but never formalized.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One GPU-day: 50 GT-scaled handheld sequences, scale-error distribution from the prior module.
kill_threshold: Kill if median scale error exceeds 15% on handheld footage or posterior intervals miss stated coverage by over 10 points.

family_fingerprint.subject_system: monocular scale estimation from capture priors

one_line_idea: Learned feature matchers win correspondence recall but lose sub-pixel precision to classical refinement: a hybrid that re-refines learned matches with classical photometric optimization will cut bundle-adjustment residuals without losing robustness.
problem: Structure-from-motion pipelines have switched to learned detectors and matchers for robustness, but reconstruction accuracy is set by sub-pixel correspondence precision, where learned heatmap peaks are coarser than classical iterative refinement.
core_hypothesis: Robustness (finding the right coarse match) and precision (localizing it to hundredths of a pixel) are separable problems: learned matchers solve the first, classical least-squares patch alignment solves the second, and chaining them will reduce reprojection residuals and camera-pose error over either alone, especially in wide-baseline and day-night conditions.
falsifiable_prediction: On reconstruction benchmarks with GT geometry, the hybrid will lower mean reprojection residual and camera-pose error versus learned-only pipelines at equal match counts, with the largest gains where learned matchers operate far from training conditions, and no measurable robustness loss.
why_important: Sub-pixel precision propagates into every measurement derived from photogrammetry; recovering classical precision on top of learned robustness upgrades mapping, inspection, and calibration pipelines at negligible cost.
why_possibly_novel: Systematic precision-robustness decomposition with a refinement-chaining study across condition strata appears missing from the learned-matching literature (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Add classical photometric refinement after public learned matchers, run full reconstruction on standard benchmarks across condition strata, and compare residuals, pose errors, and track lengths against both pure pipelines.
main_risk: Photometric refinement assumes locally affine appearance constancy, which fails under strong appearance change, exactly where learned matches are found; refinement must detect and skip such cases.
community_default_belief: Learned matchers have superseded classical correspondence machinery end to end.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The supersession evidence is recall-weighted benchmark scores that barely reward the last fraction of a pixel; the two paradigms optimize different halves of the problem and are complements, not substitutes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a GPU-day: one benchmark scene set, hybrid versus learned-only, reprojection residual comparison.
kill_threshold: Kill if the hybrid reduces mean reprojection residual by under 10% or degrades registration robustness on any stratum.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: sub-pixel refinement stage after learned matching

one_line_idea: Non-overlapping multi-camera rigs can be extrinsically calibrated to sub-degree accuracy using only a shared ground plane and per-camera odometry, removing the overlap requirement that constrains rig design.
problem: Extrinsic calibration of camera rigs requires overlapping fields of view or dedicated calibration hardware, forcing rig designs to waste coverage on overlap or accept drifting hand-measured extrinsics.
core_hypothesis: Each camera independently observes two shared references: the ground plane (constraining roll, pitch, height) and the rig's rigid motion (per-camera visual odometry must be related by the fixed extrinsics); jointly these over-constrain full six-degree extrinsics without any shared field of view, to accuracy sufficient for downstream fusion.
falsifiable_prediction: On vehicle and robot rigs with reference calibration, the ground-plane-plus-odometry solver will recover inter-camera rotations within fractions of a degree and translations within centimeters after sufficient motion diversity, with accuracy improving predictably with trajectory richness and degrading gracefully on planar-motion-only sequences.
why_important: It frees rig designers from overlap constraints (maximizing coverage per camera), enables continuous self-recalibration in the field, and replaces a maintenance procedure with software.
why_possibly_novel: Hand-eye-style calibration from odometry is classical; the joint ground-plane formulation targeting zero-overlap consumer-grade rigs with motion-richness characterization appears not established practice (unverified).
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate and then physically test rigs with known extrinsics, run per-camera odometry and ground-plane estimation, solve jointly, and map calibration error versus motion diversity and sequence length.
main_risk: Planar vehicle motion is a known degenerate case for hand-eye recovery of some components; the ground-plane constraint must be shown to break the degeneracy in practice, not just in theory.
community_default_belief: Accurate extrinsic calibration fundamentally requires overlapping views or dedicated calibration targets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The requirement is an artifact of formulating calibration as correspondence; motion and shared environmental structure are equally valid observables that non-overlapping cameras do share.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One CPU/GPU-day: simulation across motion profiles, recovered-extrinsics error versus GT.
kill_threshold: Kill if rotation error exceeds 1 degree or translation error exceeds 5 centimeters under rich motion in simulation with realistic odometry noise.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: calibration observables (ground plane plus odometry, no overlap)

one_line_idea: The self-supervised depth-flow-pose triad is not saturated: joint reliability weighting across the three estimators (each downweighting pixels where the others disagree) yields large gains in adverse conditions where each alone degrades unpredictably.
problem: Depth, flow, and pose self-supervision matured as separate pipelines with fixed loss weightings; in adverse conditions (night, rain, motion clutter) each estimator degrades differently, and static weightings propagate the worst component's errors.
core_hypothesis: The triad's mutual geometric consistency provides a per-pixel reliability signal richer than any single-model confidence: pixels where depth-flow-pose closure fails identify which estimator is failing and where, enabling adaptive reweighting that improves all three estimates in hard conditions without any new labels.
falsifiable_prediction: On adverse-condition benchmarks with GT, closure-driven adaptive weighting will improve depth error and trajectory error together by clear margins over fixed-weight joint training and over independent models, with the gains concentrated in the hard strata and near-zero cost in easy conditions.
why_important: Adverse conditions are where deployment fails and labels are scarcest; a label-free mechanism that converts cross-task disagreement into targeted robustness addresses the gap directly.
